create-adaptive-approval-emails.shortDescription: Send an approval email whose wording, approver and details change with the request.
create-adaptive-approval-emails.fullDescription: One approval flow can serve many request types if the email content is built from the item. This pattern builds the title, details and approver from the request's own values and uses the Approvals action so the decision comes back to the flow.
create-adaptive-approval-emails.problemStatement: Teams clone the same approval flow for every request type, then have to fix each copy whenever the wording or the approver changes.
whenToUse: Several request types share one approval process
The approver or the wording depends on amount, category or department
Approvers respond from Outlook or Teams
whenNotToUse: A single fixed approval with one approver
Approvals that need custom input fields, where an adaptive card in Teams fits better
stepByStepInstructions: Add columns to the list for anything the email must show, such as request type, amount and justification.
Build the approver address in a Compose so the rule is in one place.
Build the details text in a second Compose using Markdown for bold labels and blank lines.
Pass both outputs to Start and wait for an approval, and add the item link.
Branch on the outcome and write the decision and comments back to the item.
commonMistakes: Pasting HTML into Details. Approvals renders Markdown, not HTML.
Leaving the approver empty when the manager field is blank, which fails the action.
Putting the routing rule in several conditions instead of one expression.
troubleshooting: If line breaks are ignored, use two line breaks between lines. A single one is treated as a space in Markdown.
If the action fails with an invalid user, the approver expression returned null. Add a fallback with coalesce.
If approvers do not see the email, check that the Approvals notifications are not blocked and that they can also respond in the Teams Approvals app.

send-a-digest-email-grouped-by-owner.shortDescription: Send each owner one email listing all of their open items, instead of one email per item.
send-a-digest-email-grouped-by-owner.fullDescription: A scheduled flow reads the open items once, works out the distinct owners, and sends each owner a single HTML table of their items. It uses Select, union and Filter array so the only loop is one pass per owner.
send-a-digest-email-grouped-by-owner.problemStatement: Reminder flows that email once per item bury people in messages, and owners with twenty items start ignoring all of them.
whenToUse: Daily or weekly reminders of open, overdue or unassigned work
Lists where one person owns many items
Replacing a per-item reminder flow
whenNotToUse: Urgent single-item alerts that must arrive immediately
Lists with no owner column
send-a-digest-email-grouped-by-owner.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: Recurrence (weekdays 08:00) Get items Filter Query : Status eq 'Open' Top Count : 5000 Select_Owners (Map in text mode) From : @{body('Get_items')?['value']} Map : @toLower(item()?['AssignedTo']?['Email']) Compose_DistinctOwners union(body('Select_Owners'), body('Select_Owners')) Apply to each: outputs('Compose_DistinctOwners') Filter_array_Mine From : @{body('Get_items')?['value']} Condition : @equals(toLower(item()?['AssignedTo']?['Email']), items('Apply_to_each')) Select_Rows From : @{body('Filter_array_Mine')} Map : Title -> item()?['Title'] Due -> if(empty(item()?['DueDate']), '', formatDateTime(item()?['DueDate'], 'dd MMM yyyy')) Priority -> item()?['Priority']?['Value'] Create HTML table From : @{body('Select_Rows')} Send an email (V2) To : @{items('Apply_to_each')} Subject : You have @{length(body('Filter_array_Mine'))} open requests Body :

These requests are assigned to you:

@{body('Create_HTML_table')}
stepByStepInstructions: Add a Recurrence trigger and a Get items action filtered to the items that need attention.
Build a flat list of owner email addresses with Select in text mode.
Remove duplicates with union.
Loop over the distinct owners and use Filter array to pick each owner's items.
Shape the rows with Select, turn them into a table with Create HTML table, and send one email per owner.
commonMistakes: Looping over items instead of owners, which sends one email per item.
Forgetting items with no owner, which produce one blank address and a failed send.
Comparing email addresses without toLower, so the same person appears twice.
troubleshooting: If the send fails on an empty address, add a Filter array before union that removes empty values.
If the table has no borders in Outlook, add inline styles with replace() on the table output or wrap it in a styled div.
If the flow is slow, turn on concurrency for the loop. It uses no variables, so it is safe to run in parallel.

create-a-flow-run-logging-list.shortDescription: Record every important flow run in a SharePoint list so support can see what ran, for which item, and what failed.
create-a-flow-run-logging-list.fullDescription: Run history disappears after 28 days and is only visible to flow owners. A small logging list gives support staff a searchable record with a direct link to the run. This pattern defines the list and the actions that write to it.
create-a-flow-run-logging-list.problemStatement: When a user reports that nothing happened to their request, nobody outside the flow's owners can tell whether the flow ran, and old runs have already been purged.
whenToUse: Business-critical flows that other people support
Flows whose failures need follow-up
Audits that ask what was processed and when
whenNotToUse: High-volume flows, where a row per run would flood the list. Log failures only.
Personal flows with no support need
create-a-flow-run-logging-list.formulaOrCode:
List: Flow Run Log
  Title          Single line   flow name
  SourceItemId   Number        (indexed)
  SourceList     Single line
  Outcome        Choice        Succeeded | Failed | Skipped   (indexed)
  ErrorMessage   Multiple lines (plain)
  RunUrl         Hyperlink
  StartedOn      Date and time
  DurationSec    Number

Compose_RunUrl (place near the top of the flow)
  concat(
    'https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/',
    workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName'],
    '/flows/', workflow()?['name'],
    '/runs/', workflow()?['run']?['name']
  )

Scope "Try"  ... the flow's real work ...

Scope "Log success" (run after Try: is successful)
  Create item in Flow Run Log
    Title        : @{workflow()?['tags']?['flowDisplayName']}
    SourceItemId : @{triggerBody()?['ID']}
    Outcome      : Succeeded
    RunUrl       : @{outputs('Compose_RunUrl')}
    StartedOn    : @{trigger()?['startTime']}
    DurationSec  : @{div(sub(ticks(utcNow()), ticks(trigger()?['startTime'])), 10000000)}

Scope "Log failure" (run after Try: has failed, has timed out)
  Filter array
    From      : @{result('Try')}
    Condition : @equals(item()?['status'], 'Failed')
  Create item in Flow Run Log
    Outcome      : Failed
    ErrorMessage : @{coalesce(first(body('Filter_array'))?['error']?['message'], 'See run history')}
  Terminate: Failed
stepByStepInstructions: Create the logging list with the columns above and index SourceItemId and Outcome.
Add the Compose that builds the run link at the start of each flow.
Wrap the flow's work in a Try scope.
Add a success scope and a failure scope after it, each creating a log row.
End the failure scope with Terminate set to Failed so the run still shows as failed.
Add a view for failures in the last seven days and share it with support.
commonMistakes: Logging inside the Try scope, so a failure also skips the log.
Leaving the run as Succeeded after a caught failure.
Giving the log list the same permissions as the source list, which exposes error details to requesters.
troubleshooting: If the run link opens the wrong environment, check the environmentName tag. Solution flows in the default environment use a different URL prefix.
If ErrorMessage is empty, the failed action was inside a nested scope. Read result() of the inner scope instead.
If result() is not offered in the expression editor, type it by hand. It takes the name of the scope with underscores for spaces.

use-child-flows-for-shared-notification-.shortDescription: Put notification logic in one child flow and call it from every flow that needs it.
use-child-flows-for-shared-notification-.fullDescription: A child flow is a solution flow with a manual trigger that other flows call with Run a Child Flow. Moving the email and Teams logic into one child means wording, branding and channels are changed once.
use-child-flows-for-shared-notification-.problemStatement: Ten flows each contain a copy of the same notification actions, and a change to the template means editing all ten.
whenToUse: The same sequence of actions appears in several flows
Notifications that must look and behave the same everywhere
Flows that live in a solution
whenNotToUse: Flows outside solutions, which cannot call child flows
Logic used in only one flow
use-child-flows-for-shared-notification-.formulaOrCode:
Child flow: "BV Notify" (inside the solution)
  Trigger: Manually trigger a flow
    Text   Recipient      (email)
    Text   Subject
    Text   Message
    Text   Link
    Text   Channel        Email | Teams | Both

  Switch on Channel
    Email : Send an email (V2)
    Teams : Post message in a chat or channel (Chat with Flow bot)
    Both  : both actions

  Respond to a Power App or flow
    Text  Status : sent

  Settings on the child flow's details page
    Run only users > each connection: "Use this connection (name)"
    (never "Provided by run-only user")

Parent flow
  Run a Child Flow
    Child Flow : BV Notify
    Recipient  : @{triggerBody()?['Author']?['Email']}
    Subject    : Request @{triggerBody()?['Title']} approved
    Message    : Your request has been approved.
    Link       : @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']}
    Channel    : Both

  Read the result: body('Run_a_Child_Flow')?['status']
stepByStepInstructions: Create the child flow inside a solution with the manual trigger and typed inputs.
Add the shared actions and end with Respond to a Power App or flow.
Open the child flow's details page and set every connection under Run only users to use the embedded connection.
In each parent flow, add Run a Child Flow and pass the inputs.
Remove the duplicated actions from the parents.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the Respond action, so the parent waits and then fails.
Leaving connections as provided by the run-only user, which blocks the child from being called.
Changing the child's inputs without updating every parent.
troubleshooting: If Run a Child Flow is missing from the action list, the parent flow is not in a solution.
If saving the parent fails with a message about embedded connections, fix the Run only users setting on the child.
If the parent times out, the child takes too long before responding. Respond first, then continue the slow work.

build-a-scheduled-stale-item-cleanup-flo.shortDescription: Find items nobody has touched for a set number of days and archive or close them on a schedule.
build-a-scheduled-stale-item-cleanup-flo.fullDescription: A recurrence flow queries for items that are still open but have not been modified recently, marks them as archived or closed, and tells the owner. The cut-off is calculated in the query so only stale items are read.
build-a-scheduled-stale-item-cleanup-flo.problemStatement: Lists fill up with abandoned drafts and forgotten requests, which slows views and hides the work that is still active.
whenToUse: Lists with drafts or requests that are often abandoned
Keeping an active list under the 5,000 item threshold
A clear policy such as closing after 60 days without activity
whenNotToUse: Records that must be kept unchanged for compliance
Lists where Modified changes for unrelated reasons, such as bulk edits
build-a-scheduled-stale-item-cleanup-flo.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: Recurrence (weekly, Monday 06:00)

Compose_Cutoff
  addDays(utcNow(), -60, 'yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ')

Get items
  Filter Query : Status ne 'Closed' and Status ne 'Archived' and Modified lt '@{outputs('Compose_Cutoff')}'
  Order By     : Modified asc
  Top Count    : 500

Condition: length(body('Get_items')?['value']) is greater than 0

Apply to each: body('Get_items')?['value']   (Concurrency: 10)
  Update item
    Id           : @{items('Apply_to_each')?['ID']}
    Status       : Archived
    ArchivedOn   : @{utcNow()}
    ArchiveReason: No activity for 60 days

Send one summary email to the list owner
  Subject : @{length(body('Get_items')?['value'])} stale requests archived
  Body    : Create HTML table from a Select of Title, Author and Modified

Optional warning run, one week earlier
  Same query with -53 days, then email each owner:
  "This request will be archived on <date> unless it is updated."
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the rule: which statuses count as open and how many days without change count as stale.
Add Archived to the status choices and add ArchivedOn and ArchiveReason columns.
Build the cut-off date in a Compose and use it in the filter query.
Update each stale item's status instead of deleting it.
Send one summary to the list owner, and consider a warning run a week before.
commonMistakes: Deleting items outright, with no way back.
Filtering in the flow after reading the whole list.
Forgetting that the flow's own update changes Modified, which is why the status filter matters.
troubleshooting: If the query returns nothing, check the date format. SharePoint needs an ISO date in single quotes.
If the same items come back every week, the status filter does not exclude the archived value. Check the exact choice text.
If the flow triggers other flows on the list, add a trigger condition to those flows to ignore changes where Status equals Archived.

route-work-based-on-sharepoint-choice-va.shortDescription: Assign an item to the right team or person based on a choice column, using a routing list instead of hard-coded branches.
route-work-based-on-sharepoint-choice-va.fullDescription: Rather than a Switch with an address in every branch, this pattern looks up the choice value in a small routing list that holds the owner for each category. Changing who handles a category becomes a list edit, not a flow edit.
route-work-based-on-sharepoint-choice-va.problemStatement: Every reorganization means opening the flow and editing email addresses inside conditions, and nobody but the flow's author can do it.
whenToUse: Requests routed by category, department or type
Routing that changes more often than the flow should
More than three or four routes
whenNotToUse: Two fixed routes that never change, where a Condition is simpler
Routing that depends on several fields and rules, which needs a rules list or code
route-work-based-on-sharepoint-choice-va.formulaOrCode:
List: Routing
  Title        Single line   category value, exactly as in the choice column (indexed)
  Owner        Person
  TeamsChannel Single line   optional
  Active       Yes/No

Trigger: When an item is created (Requests)

Get items (Routing)
  Filter Query : Title eq '@{replace(triggerBody()?['Category']?['Value'], '''', '''''')}' and Active eq 1
  Top Count    : 1

Compose_Owner
  coalesce(
    first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['Owner']?['Email'],
    'servicedesk@contoso.com'
  )

Update item (Requests)
  Id               : @{triggerBody()?['ID']}
  AssignedTo Claims: @{outputs('Compose_Owner')}
  Status           : Assigned

Send an email (V2)
  To      : @{outputs('Compose_Owner')}
  Subject : New @{triggerBody()?['Category']?['Value']} request: @{triggerBody()?['Title']}

Trigger condition (Settings) so the update does not retrigger on create-and-modify flows
  @empty(triggerBody()?['AssignedTo'])
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Routing list with one row per choice value.
Read the item's choice value with ?['Value'] and look it up in the Routing list.
Fall back to a default owner when no row matches.
Write the owner to the item and notify them.
Give the business owner edit access to the Routing list.
commonMistakes: Reading the choice column without ?['Value'], which returns an object.
No default route, so an unmapped category fails the flow.
Routing values that differ from the choice text by a space or capital letter.
troubleshooting: If the lookup returns nothing, compare the routing Title with the choice value character for character.
If a category containing an apostrophe breaks the filter, keep the replace() shown above, which doubles single quotes.
If the person column will not update, pass the email address to the Claims field of the column.

use-switch-control-for-status-based-flow.shortDescription: Run a different set of actions for each status value with one Switch instead of nested conditions.
use-switch-control-for-status-based-flow.fullDescription: Switch compares one value against several cases and runs the matching branch. For status-driven flows it is flatter and easier to read than conditions inside conditions, and the default case catches values nobody planned for.
use-switch-control-for-status-based-flow.problemStatement: A flow has conditions nested four levels deep to handle five statuses, and adding a sixth means restructuring the whole thing.
whenToUse: One value decides between three or more paths
Status, type or category driven logic
Flows that must do something sensible for unexpected values
whenNotToUse: Comparisons such as greater than or contains. Switch only tests equality.
Two outcomes, where a Condition is clearer
use-switch-control-for-status-based-flow.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: When an item is created or modified (Requests)
  Trigger condition: @not(equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Draft'))

Switch
  On : @{triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value']}

  Case "Submitted"
    Start and wait for an approval ...
  Case "Approved"
    Send an email to the requester
    Create a Planner task for fulfilment
  Case "Rejected"
    Send an email with the approver's comments
  Case "On Hold"
    Post a message to the team channel
  Default
    Send an email to the flow owner:
    "Unhandled status '@{triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value']}' on item @{triggerBody()?['ID']}"

Switch on a calculated value (ranges)
  On : @{if(greater(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 10000), 'High',
          if(greater(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 1000), 'Medium', 'Low'))}
  Cases: High | Medium | Low
stepByStepInstructions: Add a Switch and set On to the status text, using ?['Value'] for a choice column.
Add one case per status, typing the value exactly as stored.
Move the actions for each status into its case.
Add a Default case that reports unexpected values.
For ranges, calculate a label first and switch on the label.
commonMistakes: Case values that differ in capitals or spacing from the stored value. Cases are case-sensitive.
Leaving Default empty, so new statuses pass silently.
Trying to use an expression as a case value. Cases must be constants.
troubleshooting: If every run goes to Default, output the On value in a Compose and compare it with the case text.
If you need the same actions for two statuses, map both to one label in an expression and switch on that.
If the flow runs when it should not, pair the Switch with a trigger condition so it only starts for relevant statuses.

parse-semicolon-separated-emails-into-re.shortDescription: Turn text such as 'a@x.com; b@x.com' into a clean recipient list, or into individual addresses to loop over.
parse-semicolon-separated-emails-into-re.fullDescription: Addresses arrive in a text column separated by semicolons, commas or line breaks, with stray spaces and blanks. This pattern normalizes the separators, splits the text, trims each entry, removes blanks and duplicates, and joins the result for the To field.
parse-semicolon-separated-emails-into-re.problemStatement: An email action fails with an invalid recipient because the stored list has a trailing semicolon, a space after a comma or the same address twice.
whenToUse: Recipient lists stored in a text column or a settings list
Addresses pasted by users
Sending one email per address from a combined field
whenNotToUse: Multi-person columns, which already provide an array
Distribution lists, which should be a group address
parse-semicolon-separated-emails-into-re.formulaOrCode:
Compose_Raw
  coalesce(triggerBody()?['NotifyEmails'], '')

Compose_Normalized  (commas and line breaks become semicolons)
  replace(
    replace(
      replace(outputs('Compose_Raw'), ',', ';'),
      decodeUriComponent('%0A'), ';'),
    decodeUriComponent('%0D'), '')

Select_Trimmed  (Map in text mode)
  From : @{split(outputs('Compose_Normalized'), ';')}
  Map  : @toLower(trim(item()))

Filter_array_Valid
  From      : @{body('Select_Trimmed')}
  Condition : @and(not(empty(item())), contains(item(), '@'))

Compose_Distinct
  union(body('Filter_array_Valid'), body('Filter_array_Valid'))

Send an email (V2)
  To : @{join(outputs('Compose_Distinct'), ';')}

Or one email each
  Apply to each: outputs('Compose_Distinct')
    To : @{items('Apply_to_each')}

Guard: only send when there is at least one address
  greater(length(outputs('Compose_Distinct')), 0)
stepByStepInstructions: Read the text with coalesce so an empty column becomes an empty string.
Replace commas and line breaks with semicolons.
Split on the semicolon and trim each entry with Select in text mode.
Remove blanks and anything without an at sign, then remove duplicates with union.
Join the list for the To field, or loop over it.
commonMistakes: Splitting without trimming, so addresses keep a leading space.
Not handling a trailing separator, which creates an empty entry.
Calling split on null when the column is empty.
troubleshooting: If split fails, the input was null. Keep the coalesce in the first step.
If the send fails with an invalid recipient, output the final list in a Compose and look for hidden characters or missing domains.
If line breaks are not replaced, the text uses a different break. Replace both %0A and %0D as shown.

create-an-approval-audit-trail-in-sharep.shortDescription: Write every approval decision to a separate history list with who decided, when, and what they said.
create-an-approval-audit-trail-in-sharep.fullDescription: The Approvals connector keeps its own history, but it is hard to report on and tied to the environment. This pattern records each response in a SharePoint list linked to the request, so the trail is visible next to the item and survives flow changes.
create-an-approval-audit-trail-in-sharep.problemStatement: Auditors ask who approved a request and when, and the only evidence is a status column that has since been overwritten.
whenToUse: Approvals that are audited or disputed
Multi-stage approvals where each stage must be visible
Requests whose status changes after approval
whenNotToUse: Informal sign-offs with no record-keeping need
Regulated records that must live in a dedicated records system
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Approval History list and index RequestId.
After the approval action, loop over its responses and create one history row per response.
Update the request with the overall outcome and the last decision details.
Restrict edit rights on the history list to the flow's account.
Add a view of history to the request's display form or app, filtered by RequestId.
commonMistakes: Storing only the final status on the request, which loses earlier decisions.
Letting everyone edit the history list.
Recording the flow owner as the approver instead of the responder.
troubleshooting: If comments are empty, the approver left none. Store a short note such as No comment given, so the column is not misread as missing data.
If only one row is written for an everyone-must-approve approval, loop over responses instead of reading the summary fields.
If the person column fails to save, pass the responder's email to the Claims field.

retry-transient-sharepoint-connector-fai.shortDescription: Configure retry policies and a manual retry loop so brief SharePoint errors do not fail the whole flow.
retry-transient-sharepoint-connector-fai.fullDescription: Throttling and gateway errors from SharePoint are usually gone a few seconds later. Each action has a retry policy that can be tuned, and for cases the policy does not cover, a Do until loop with a delay gives full control.
retry-transient-sharepoint-connector-fai.problemStatement: A flow that works all week fails on Monday morning with 429 or 502 errors when many flows run at once, and someone has to resubmit runs by hand.
whenToUse: Flows that fail intermittently with 429, 502, 503 or 504
High-volume flows against one site
Updates that may hit a save conflict
whenNotToUse: Errors that will never succeed on retry, such as 400 or 403
Actions that are not safe to repeat, such as Create item, unless you check for the item first
retry-transient-sharepoint-connector-fai.formulaOrCode:
1. Tune the built-in retry policy
   Action > Settings > Retry Policy
     Type             : Exponential Interval
     Count            : 6
     Interval         : PT10S
     Minimum Interval : PT10S
     Maximum Interval : PT5M
   The default is 4 exponential retries. Retries apply to 408, 429 and 5xx.

2. Reduce the load that causes throttling
   Apply to each > Settings > Concurrency: On, Degree of Parallelism: 5
   Trigger > Settings > Concurrency: On, limit 5

3. Manual retry for errors the policy does not retry (for example 409 conflict)
   Initialize variable  varDone   Boolean  false
   Initialize variable  varTries  Integer  0

   Do until  variables('varDone') is equal to true     (Limit: Count 5, Timeout PT15M)
     Scope "Attempt"
       Get item                (re-read to get the current version)
       Update item
     Set variable varDone = true          (run after Attempt: is successful)
     Increment variable varTries          (run after Attempt: has failed, has timed out)
     Delay  @{mul(variables('varTries'), 20)} seconds   (same run-after)

   Condition after the loop: variables('varDone') is false -> Terminate Failed
stepByStepInstructions: Open run history and note which action fails and with which status code.
For 429 and 5xx errors, raise the retry count and interval on that action.
Lower loop and trigger concurrency so the flow sends fewer requests at once.
For conflicts, wrap the read and update in a Do until loop with a growing delay.
Fail the run clearly if the loop ends without success.
commonMistakes: Retrying Create item without checking whether the first attempt actually succeeded, which creates duplicates.
Setting concurrency to 50 and then adding retries to cope with the throttling it causes.
Retrying permission and validation errors, which never succeed.
troubleshooting: If the run shows many retries and then fails, the outage lasted longer than the policy. Increase the maximum interval.
If you see 429 with a Retry-After header, the connector already waits for it. Reduce the request rate rather than adding more retries.
If duplicates appear, add a unique key column and query for it before creating.

use-terminate-action-for-controlled-flow.shortDescription: End a run on purpose with the right status and a clear message when the data is not fit to process.
use-terminate-action-for-controlled-flow.fullDescription: Terminate stops a flow immediately and marks the run as Succeeded, Failed or Cancelled. Used after validation or inside an error handler, it makes run history tell the truth and gives support a readable reason.
use-terminate-action-for-controlled-flow.problemStatement: A flow catches its own errors and finishes as Succeeded, so failed requests go unnoticed, or it fails deep inside with a cryptic connector message when the real cause was missing input.
whenToUse: Input validation at the start of a flow
The end of a catch scope, so a handled error still shows as failed
Stopping early when there is nothing to do
whenNotToUse: Inside Apply to each when only that iteration should stop. Terminate ends the whole run.
When later clean-up actions must still run
use-terminate-action-for-controlled-flow.formulaOrCode:
1. Validate early and stop with a reason
   Condition: empty(triggerBody()?['Manager']?['Email'])
     Yes:
       Update item   Status = Needs attention
                     FlowMessage = Manager is missing
       Terminate
         Status  : Failed
         Code    : MissingManager
         Message : Request @{triggerBody()?['ID']} has no manager, so approval could not start.

2. Nothing to do: stop quietly
   Condition: equals(length(body('Get_items')?['value']), 0)
     Yes:
       Terminate
         Status : Cancelled        (keeps failure reports clean)

3. After a catch scope: report, then fail
   Scope "Try"   ...
   Scope "Catch" (run after Try: has failed, has timed out)
     Filter array
       From      : @{result('Try')}
       Condition : @equals(item()?['status'], 'Failed')
     Send an email to support with
       @{first(body('Filter_array'))?['name']}: @{first(body('Filter_array'))?['error']?['message']}
     Terminate
       Status  : Failed
       Code    : @{coalesce(first(body('Filter_array'))?['code'], 'Unhandled')}
       Message : @{coalesce(first(body('Filter_array'))?['error']?['message'], 'See run history')}
stepByStepInstructions: List the inputs the flow cannot work without.
Add conditions at the top that check them, and Terminate as Failed with a specific code and message.
Use Cancelled for runs that have nothing to process.
End every catch scope with Terminate set to Failed.
Filter run history by Failed to confirm that only real problems appear.
commonMistakes: Catching errors and leaving the run as Succeeded.
Using Failed for normal no-work runs, which hides real failures in noise.
Writing a generic message that does not name the item or the missing value.
troubleshooting: If Terminate inside a loop ends the run too early, set a flag variable in the loop and terminate after it.
If the run shows Succeeded despite Terminate, another branch ran in parallel and finished first. Check the run-after settings.
If failure alerts are too noisy, change expected stops from Failed to Cancelled.

build-a-file-naming-standard-flow.shortDescription: Rename uploaded files to a standard pattern built from their metadata.
build-a-file-naming-standard-flow.fullDescription: When a file is added to a library, this flow builds a name from its properties, strips characters SharePoint does not allow, and renames the file with a REST call. A trigger condition stops the flow from running again on its own rename.
build-a-file-naming-standard-flow.problemStatement: Libraries fill with files called Scan001.pdf and Final v2 (3).docx, and people cannot tell what a file is without opening it.
whenToUse: Libraries where files are uploaded with arbitrary names
A naming rule that can be built from metadata
Files that other systems find by name
whenNotToUse: Files with links already shared by name-based URL, which a rename can break
Libraries where users choose meaningful names themselves
build-a-file-naming-standard-flow.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: When a file is created (properties only)
  Trigger condition (Settings):
    @not(startsWith(triggerBody()?['{FilenameWithExtension}'], 'REQ-'))

Compose_Extension
  last(split(triggerBody()?['{FilenameWithExtension}'], '.'))

Compose_CleanTitle   (remove characters SharePoint rejects, collapse spaces)
  replace(replace(replace(replace(replace(replace(replace(replace(replace(
    trim(coalesce(triggerBody()?['DocumentTitle'], triggerBody()?['{Name}'])),
    '"', ''), '*', ''), ':', ''), '<', ''), '>', ''), '?', ''), '/', '-'), '\\', '-'), '|', '-')

Compose_NewName
  concat(
    'REQ-', triggerBody()?['RequestId'], '_',
    triggerBody()?['DocType']?['Value'], '_',
    replace(outputs('Compose_CleanTitle'), ' ', '-'), '_',
    formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'yyyyMMdd'),
    '.', outputs('Compose_Extension')
  )

Send an HTTP request to SharePoint
  Method  : POST
  Uri     : _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Documents')/items(@{triggerBody()?['ID']})/validateUpdateListItem
  Headers : Accept: application/json;odata=nometadata
            Content-Type: application/json;odata=nometadata
  Body    :
  {
    "formValues": [
      { "FieldName": "FileLeafRef", "FieldValue": "@{outputs('Compose_NewName')}" }
    ]
  }
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the naming rule and which metadata columns it uses.
Add a trigger condition that skips files already matching the standard.
Build the extension, a cleaned title and the new name in Compose actions.
Rename by setting FileLeafRef with Send an HTTP request to SharePoint.
Make the metadata columns required, so the name can always be built.
commonMistakes: No trigger condition, so the rename retriggers the flow.
Dropping the file extension from the new name.
Leaving characters such as slash, colon or question mark in the name.
troubleshooting: If the request returns 200 but the name is unchanged, read the response body. It reports the field error, such as an invalid character or a duplicate name.
If two files would get the same name, add the item ID or a time to the pattern.
If required metadata is empty at creation, wait for it with a trigger on modified and a condition that the columns are filled.

notify-when-a-project-health-turns-red.shortDescription: Alert the right people once when a status changes to red, not on every later edit.
notify-when-a-project-health-turns-red.fullDescription: The modified trigger fires for any change. This pattern stores the previously notified value on the item and uses a trigger condition so the flow starts only when health is red and has not yet been announced, then resets when it leaves red.
notify-when-a-project-health-turns-red.problemStatement: A red-status alert flow sends the same warning every time someone edits a red project, so people mute it and miss the next real change.
whenToUse: Alerts on a status changing to a specific value
Escalations that should happen once per occurrence
Lists edited frequently
whenNotToUse: Alerts that should repeat as reminders, which belong in a scheduled flow
Lists with versioning where you prefer to compare versions
notify-when-a-project-health-turns-red.formulaOrCode:
Columns on Projects
  Health          Choice   Green | Amber | Red
  HealthNotified  Choice   Green | Amber | Red   (hidden from forms)

Flow 1: alert when it turns red
  Trigger: When an item is created or modified
  Trigger condition:
    @and(
      equals(triggerBody()?['Health']?['Value'], 'Red'),
      not(equals(triggerBody()?['HealthNotified']?['Value'], 'Red'))
    )

  Post message in a chat or channel (Teams)
    @{triggerBody()?['Title']} is now RED.
    Owner: @{triggerBody()?['ProjectManager']?['DisplayName']}
    Reason: @{coalesce(triggerBody()?['HealthComment'], 'No comment given')}
    @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']}

  Send an email (V2) to the sponsor
    Importance: High

  Update item
    HealthNotified : Red

Flow 2: reset when it leaves red
  Trigger condition:
    @and(
      not(equals(triggerBody()?['Health']?['Value'], 'Red')),
      equals(triggerBody()?['HealthNotified']?['Value'], 'Red')
    )
  Update item
    HealthNotified : @{triggerBody()?['Health']?['Value']}
stepByStepInstructions: Add a HealthNotified column to hold the last value that was announced.
Add the trigger condition so the flow runs only when health is red and has not been announced.
Send the Teams message and email with the item link and the reason.
Set HealthNotified to Red as the last step.
Add the small second flow that resets the marker when health improves.
commonMistakes: Alerting on every modification of a red item.
Updating the item without a trigger condition, causing a loop.
Showing the marker column on forms, where users change it.
troubleshooting: If the flow never triggers, test the trigger condition expression in a Compose in a test flow. A typing error makes it silently false.
If alerts repeat, the final update failed. Check that the flow account can edit the item.
If you need the previous value in the message, store it in a second column before the update or read the item's version history.

create-monthly-portfolio-summary-emails.shortDescription: Send a monthly email with counts by status, the top items needing attention and a link to the full view.
create-monthly-portfolio-summary-emails.fullDescription: A recurrence flow reads the active items once, counts them by status with Filter array, builds a short table of the items that most need attention, and sends a single formatted email to leadership.
create-monthly-portfolio-summary-emails.problemStatement: Someone spends the first morning of every month copying numbers from a list into an email by hand.
whenToUse: Regular summaries for managers or sponsors
Lists with a status or health column
Reports that only need counts and a short list
whenNotToUse: Analysis with trends and charts, which belongs in Power BI
Lists too large to read in one Get items call
create-monthly-portfolio-summary-emails.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: Recurrence (monthly, day 1, 07:00) Get items (Projects) Filter Query : Status ne 'Closed' Top Count : 5000 Filter_array_Red @equals(item()?['Health']?['Value'], 'Red') Filter_array_Amber @equals(item()?['Health']?['Value'], 'Amber') Filter_array_Green @equals(item()?['Health']?['Value'], 'Green') Select_RedRows From : @{take(body('Filter_array_Red'), 10)} Map : Project -> item()?['Title'] Owner -> item()?['ProjectManager']?['DisplayName'] Due -> if(empty(item()?['TargetDate']), '', formatDateTime(item()?['TargetDate'], 'dd MMM yyyy')) Reason -> coalesce(item()?['HealthComment'], '') Create HTML table From: @{body('Select_RedRows')} Compose_Table (basic styling for Outlook) replace( replace(body('Create_HTML_table'), '', '
'), '
', '') Send an email (V2) Subject : Portfolio summary for @{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), -1), 'MMMM yyyy')} Body :

@{length(body('Get_items')?['value'])} active projects: @{length(body('Filter_array_Red'))} red, @{length(body('Filter_array_Amber'))} amber, @{length(body('Filter_array_Green'))} green.

Red projects:

@{outputs('Compose_Table')}

Open the full list
stepByStepInstructions: Add a monthly Recurrence trigger and a Get items action for active items.
Add one Filter array per status and use length() for the counts.
Shape the top rows with Select and build a table with Create HTML table.
Add inline styles with replace so the table reads well in Outlook.
Send one email with the counts, the table and a link to a list view.
commonMistakes: Counting with a loop and variables instead of Filter array and length.
Sending the whole list as a table, which nobody reads.
Naming the wrong month. A run on the first reports on the previous month.
troubleshooting: If the counts do not add up, some items have an empty health value. Add a count for blanks.
If Outlook strips the styling, use inline styles on table cells as shown instead of a style block.
If Get items returns only 100 rows, set Top Count or turn on pagination.

build-a-small-business-pto-request-workf.shortDescription: Handle time-off requests with a list, a manager approval and a shared calendar entry.
build-a-small-business-pto-request-workf.fullDescription: A complete small-team leave process: a SharePoint list for requests, a flow that works out the manager, asks for approval, writes the decision back and adds approved leave to a shared calendar.
build-a-small-business-pto-request-workf.problemStatement: Time off is agreed by email or chat, nobody has a single view of who is away, and requests get lost.
whenToUse: Small teams without an HR system
Organizations where manager data is kept in Microsoft 365
A simple approve or reject process
whenNotToUse: Leave balances and accrual rules, which need an HR system or a more complete app
Organizations where managers are not set in the directory
stepByStepInstructions: Create the list with the columns and the date validation formula.
Look up the requester's manager and fall back to a shared mailbox when none is set.
Start the approval with the dates formatted for reading.
Write the outcome, approver and comments back to the item.
Create an all-day event in a shared calendar for approved requests, ending the day after the last day of leave.
Email the requester the result.
commonMistakes: Ending the all-day event on the last day, which makes the calendar show one day short.
Failing when a person has no manager in the directory.
Letting requesters edit Status themselves. Hide it on the form and restrict it with permissions or the flow.
troubleshooting: If Get manager fails, the user has no manager set. Keep the run-after and fallback shown above.
If the event is on the wrong day, the date-only value was converted from UTC. Pass the date as yyyy-MM-dd.
If the approval never arrives, check that the approver address is a real mailbox and not a group.

build-an-expense-reimbursement-request-w.shortDescription: Route expense claims by amount, require a receipt, and notify finance once approved.
build-an-expense-reimbursement-request-w.fullDescription: An expense process built on a SharePoint list: the flow checks for an attached receipt, routes to the manager and then to finance above a threshold, records each decision, and notifies finance with the details needed to pay.
build-an-expense-reimbursement-request-w.problemStatement: Expense claims arrive by email with missing receipts, approval depends on who remembers to forward them, and finance re-types the details.
whenToUse: Small organizations without an expense system
Claims that need one or two levels of approval
Receipts kept with the claim
whenNotToUse: Card reconciliation, mileage rates and tax rules, which need dedicated software
High volumes of claims
build-an-expense-reimbursement-request-w.formulaOrCode:
List: Expense Claims
  Title         Single line      what the expense was for
  ExpenseDate   Date
  Amount        Currency
  Category      Choice           Travel | Meals | Supplies | Other
  CostCentre    Single line
  Status        Choice           Submitted | Needs receipt | Manager approved |
                                 Approved | Rejected | Paid
  DecisionNote  Multiple lines
  Attachments   enabled (receipt)

Trigger: When an item is created
  Trigger condition: @equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Submitted')

Get attachments
Condition: length(body('Get_attachments')) is equal to 0
  Yes: Update item Status = Needs receipt
       Email the requester asking them to attach the receipt and set Status back to Submitted
       Terminate (Cancelled)

Get manager (V2) for the requester
Approval 1: manager
  Details: **@{triggerBody()?['Category']?['Value']}**  @{formatNumber(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 'C2', 'en-GB')}
           on @{formatDateTime(triggerBody()?['ExpenseDate'], 'd MMM yyyy')}
  Rejected -> Update item Status = Rejected, DecisionNote = comments, email requester, Terminate

Update item Status = Manager approved

Condition: Amount is greater than 500
  Yes: Approval 2 assigned to finance-approvers@contoso.com
       Rejected -> Status = Rejected, email requester, Terminate

Update item Status = Approved

Send an email (V2) to finance@contoso.com
  Subject : Expense to pay: @{triggerBody()?['Author']?['DisplayName']} @{formatNumber(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 'C2', 'en-GB')}
  Body    : claimant, cost centre, category, date, amount, link to the item
  Attachments: loop Get attachment content and add each file
stepByStepInstructions: Create the list with attachments enabled and the status values above.
Check for a receipt first and stop with a clear request when it is missing.
Route to the manager, then to finance when the amount is above your threshold.
Update the status after each step so the list always shows where the claim is.
Send finance one email with everything needed to pay, including the receipt.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding the threshold in several places. Keep it in one Compose or a settings list.
Letting the claimant approve their own claim when they are also the manager on record.
Not telling the requester why a claim was rejected.
troubleshooting: If the flow cannot see attachments, they were added after creation. Trigger on modified with a status of Submitted instead.
If currency shows the wrong symbol, pass a locale to formatNumber.
If the manager is also the claimant, compare the two addresses and route to finance instead.

create-a-vendor-onboarding-workflow-pack.shortDescription: Collect vendor details, run reviews in parallel, and create the onboarding tasks once every review passes.
create-a-vendor-onboarding-workflow-pack.fullDescription: Vendor onboarding needs several teams to check different things. This pattern uses a request list, parallel approvals for finance, security and legal, and a templated set of follow-up tasks created only when all reviews are approved.
create-a-vendor-onboarding-workflow-pack.problemStatement: New vendors wait weeks because reviews happen one after another by email, and nobody can see which review is holding things up.
whenToUse: Onboarding that needs sign-off from several teams
Reviews that do not depend on each other
A repeatable checklist after approval
whenNotToUse: One-person approvals
Processes that already run in a procurement system
create-a-vendor-onboarding-workflow-pack.formulaOrCode:
List: Vendor Requests
  Title (vendor name) | ContactEmail | ServiceType (Choice) | AnnualSpend (Currency)
  HandlesPersonalData (Yes/No) | Status (Choice: Submitted, In review, Approved, Rejected)
  FinanceReview / SecurityReview / LegalReview  (Choice: Pending, Approved, Rejected, Not required)

List: Onboarding Task Templates
  Title | OwnerEmail | DueInDays (Number) | Order (Number)

Trigger: When an item is created
Update item: Status = In review

Parallel branches
  Branch A  Start and wait for an approval -> finance@contoso.com
            Update item FinanceReview = outcome
  Branch B  Condition: HandlesPersonalData is true
              Yes: approval -> security@contoso.com, SecurityReview = outcome
              No : SecurityReview = Not required
  Branch C  Condition: AnnualSpend is greater than 25000
              Yes: approval -> legal@contoso.com, LegalReview = outcome
              No : LegalReview = Not required

After all branches (run after: is successful for each)
  Get item (re-read the three review columns)
  Compose_AnyRejected
    or(
      equals(body('Get_item')?['FinanceReview']?['Value'], 'Rejected'),
      equals(body('Get_item')?['SecurityReview']?['Value'], 'Rejected'),
      equals(body('Get_item')?['LegalReview']?['Value'], 'Rejected')
    )

  Condition: Compose_AnyRejected is true
    Yes: Status = Rejected, email the requester with which review rejected and why
    No : Status = Approved
         Get items (Onboarding Task Templates, Order By Order)
         Apply to each template
           Create a task (Planner)
             Title    : @{triggerBody()?['Title']}: @{items('Apply_to_each')?['Title']}
             Due date : @{addDays(utcNow(), int(items('Apply_to_each')?['DueInDays']))}
             Assigned : @{items('Apply_to_each')?['OwnerEmail']}
stepByStepInstructions: Create the request list with one review column per team.
Create a task template list so the checklist can change without editing the flow.
Add parallel branches, one per review, each writing its own outcome to the item.
After the branches, re-read the item and decide the overall result.
On approval, create one Planner task per template row.
commonMistakes: Running reviews one after another when they are independent.
Having every branch update the same Status column, so the last one to finish wins.
Hard-coding the task list in the flow.
troubleshooting: If the step after the branches runs too early, set its run-after to depend on the last action of every branch.
If a branch update fails with a conflict, each branch should update only its own column. Add a retry policy as a safeguard.
If Planner tasks are created without an owner, the template's address is not a member of the plan's group.

create-a-power-automate-flow-documentati.shortDescription: Document each production flow on one page that support can use without opening the designer.
create-a-power-automate-flow-documentati.fullDescription: A fixed template for flow documentation covering purpose, trigger, connections, data touched, failure handling and ownership. Kept in a list or a wiki page per flow, it turns a personal automation into something a team can support.
create-a-power-automate-flow-documentati.problemStatement: The only person who understands a critical flow is on holiday when it fails, and nobody else knows what it does or what is safe to change.
whenToUse: Flows the business depends on
Before handing a flow to a support team
Solution releases
whenNotToUse: Personal productivity flows
As a substitute for clear action names inside the flow
create-a-power-automate-flow-documentati.formulaOrCode:
Flow documentation template

1. Summary
   Name              : BV Requests - Notify approver on submit
   Purpose           : one sentence in business terms
   Business owner    : name and team
   Technical owner   : name, plus a backup
   Environment / solution : Prod / BV Requests

2. Trigger
   Type              : SharePoint - When an item is created or modified
   Source            : site URL, list name
   Trigger condition : @equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Submitted')
   Expected volume   : about 40 runs a day

3. What it does (5 to 10 numbered steps, plain language)

4. Connections
   Connector | Connection reference | Account | Why it is needed

5. Data
   Reads             : lists, tables, mailboxes
   Writes            : lists, columns, files, messages sent
   Personal data     : yes/no, which fields

6. Configuration
   Environment variables : name, meaning, current value location
   Hard-coded values     : any that remain, and why

7. Failure handling
   Error handling    : Try/Catch scopes, what is logged and where
   Alerts            : who is told, how
   Safe to resubmit? : yes/no, and what to check first
   Known failures    : symptom -> cause -> fix

8. Dependencies
   Child flows, other flows triggered by its updates, apps that call it

9. Change log
   Date | Version | Change | Who
stepByStepInstructions: Copy the template into a list item or page for each production flow.
Fill in the summary and trigger first. They answer most support questions.
Describe the steps in plain language, not action names.
Record whether the flow is safe to resubmit and what to check first.
Link the page from the flow's description field.
Update the change log with every release.
commonMistakes: Pasting screenshots of the designer instead of explaining what the flow does.
Leaving out whether a failed run can be resubmitted safely.
Writing the document once and never updating it.
troubleshooting: If documents go stale, make updating the page part of the release checklist.
If nobody can find the page, put its link in the flow's description, which shows on the flow's details page.
If the template feels too long for small flows, keep sections 1, 2, 7 and 9 as the minimum.

route-approvals-by-request-amount.shortDescription: Send small requests to the manager and larger ones to more senior approvers, using thresholds kept in a list.
route-approvals-by-request-amount.fullDescription: Amount-based routing is the most common approval rule. This pattern reads the thresholds from a small list, picks the highest tier the amount reaches, and runs the approval stages in order up to that tier.
route-approvals-by-request-amount.problemStatement: Spending limits are written into flow conditions, so a change in policy means a developer has to edit and retest the flow.
whenToUse: Purchase, expense or discount approvals with spending limits
Limits that finance changes from time to time
Two or more approval tiers
whenNotToUse: A single approver for every amount
Rules that depend on more than amount, which need a fuller rules list
route-approvals-by-request-amount.formulaOrCode:
List: Approval Tiers
  Title (tier name) | MinAmount (Number, indexed) | Approver (Person) | Order (Number)
  Manager   |     0 | (blank: use requester's manager) | 1
  Director  |  5000 | director@contoso.com            | 2
  CFO       | 25000 | cfo@contoso.com                 | 3

Get items (Approval Tiers)
  Filter Query : MinAmount le @{coalesce(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 0)}
  Order By     : Order asc

Apply to each tier (Concurrency: off, so stages run in order)
  Compose_Approver
    coalesce(
      items('Apply_to_each')?['Approver']?['Email'],
      outputs('Get_manager_(V2)')?['body/mail']
    )
  Start and wait for an approval
    Title       : @{items('Apply_to_each')?['Title']} approval: @{triggerBody()?['Title']} (@{formatNumber(triggerBody()?['Amount'], 'N2')})
    Assigned to : @{outputs('Compose_Approver')}
  Condition: outcome is equal to Reject
    Yes: Update item Status = Rejected, RejectedAt = tier name
         Terminate (Succeeded)

After the loop: Update item Status = Approved
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Approval Tiers list with a minimum amount and approver per tier.
Query the tiers whose minimum is at or below the request amount, in order.
Loop through them one at a time, starting an approval for each.
Stop at the first rejection and record which tier rejected.
Mark the request approved when the loop completes.
commonMistakes: Turning on loop concurrency, which sends all tiers at once.
Comparing a currency column as text.
Hard-coding thresholds in conditions.
troubleshooting: If no tier is returned, the amount is empty or below every minimum. Keep a tier with a minimum of zero.
If a higher tier is skipped, check the Order values and that the filter uses le, not lt.
If the manager tier fails, the requester has no manager set. Add a fallback approver.

route-approvals-by-department-code.shortDescription: Find the approver for a request from the requester's department, using a department list.
route-approvals-by-department-code.fullDescription: Departments change heads more often than flows should change. This pattern reads the requester's department from their profile or from the item, looks up that department's approver in a list, and falls back to a default.
route-approvals-by-department-code.problemStatement: The flow sends approvals to whoever was head of department when it was built, and updates lag behind every reorganization.
whenToUse: Approvals owned by department heads or cost-centre owners
Organizations where department is set on user profiles
More than a few departments
whenNotToUse: Approval by direct line manager, where Get manager is enough
Departments that are not recorded anywhere reliable
route-approvals-by-department-code.formulaOrCode:
List: Departments
  Title (department code, indexed) | DepartmentName | Approver (Person) | Deputy (Person)

Get user profile (V2)
  User (UPN) : @{triggerBody()?['Author']?['Email']}

Compose_DeptCode   (item value wins over the profile)
  coalesce(triggerBody()?['DepartmentCode'], outputs('Get_user_profile_(V2)')?['body/department'], '')

Get items (Departments)
  Filter Query : Title eq '@{replace(outputs('Compose_DeptCode'), '''', '''''')}'
  Top Count    : 1

Compose_Approver
  coalesce(
    first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['Approver']?['Email'],
    'approvals@contoso.com'
  )

Compose_FinalApprover   (never route to the requester)
  if(
    equals(toLower(outputs('Compose_Approver')), toLower(triggerBody()?['Author']?['Email'])),
    coalesce(first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['Deputy']?['Email'], 'approvals@contoso.com'),
    outputs('Compose_Approver')
  )

Start and wait for an approval
  Assigned to : @{outputs('Compose_FinalApprover')}
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Departments list keyed by department code.
Read the department from the item, falling back to the requester's profile.
Look up the department's approver and fall back to a shared approvals mailbox.
Swap to the deputy when the approver is the requester.
Start the approval with the final address.
commonMistakes: Relying on the profile's department text matching the list exactly without checking.
Letting a head of department approve their own request.
No fallback for an unknown department.
troubleshooting: If the lookup misses, output the department value and compare it with the list. Profile values often carry extra text such as a location.
If Get user profile fails for guests, use the item's department column for them.
If approvals reach the shared mailbox often, add the missing departments to the list.

route-approvals-by-project-phase.shortDescription: Change who approves as a project moves from initiation to delivery to closure.
route-approvals-by-project-phase.fullDescription: Different phases need different sign-off. This pattern stores the approver role for each phase in a list and resolves that role to a person from the project record, so the flow needs no change when phases or roles are adjusted.
route-approvals-by-project-phase.problemStatement: Every phase gate has its own flow with its own hard-coded approver, and they drift apart over time.
whenToUse: Stage-gate processes
Projects where sponsor, manager and owner are recorded per project
Approver depends on phase, not on amount
whenNotToUse: Processes with one phase
Projects that do not record their roles as people columns
route-approvals-by-project-phase.formulaOrCode:
List: Phase Approvals
  Title (phase, indexed)  | ApproverRole (Choice: Sponsor, ProjectManager, PMO, BusinessOwner)
  Initiation  | Sponsor
  Planning    | PMO
  Delivery    | ProjectManager
  Closure     | BusinessOwner

Projects list people columns: Sponsor, ProjectManager, BusinessOwner

Get item (Projects)   Id: @{triggerBody()?['ProjectId']}

Get items (Phase Approvals)
  Filter Query : Title eq '@{body('Get_item')?['Phase']?['Value']}'
  Top Count    : 1

Compose_Role
  coalesce(first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['ApproverRole']?['Value'], 'PMO')

Compose_Approver
  if(equals(outputs('Compose_Role'), 'Sponsor'),        body('Get_item')?['Sponsor']?['Email'],
  if(equals(outputs('Compose_Role'), 'ProjectManager'), body('Get_item')?['ProjectManager']?['Email'],
  if(equals(outputs('Compose_Role'), 'BusinessOwner'),  body('Get_item')?['BusinessOwner']?['Email'],
     'pmo@contoso.com')))

Start and wait for an approval
  Title       : @{body('Get_item')?['Phase']?['Value']} gate: @{body('Get_item')?['Title']}
  Assigned to : @{coalesce(outputs('Compose_Approver'), 'pmo@contoso.com')}
stepByStepInstructions: Record sponsor, project manager and business owner as people columns on the project.
Create the Phase Approvals list mapping each phase to a role.
Read the project, look up the role for its current phase, and resolve the role to a person.
Fall back to the PMO mailbox when the role is empty.
Start the approval and write the result to the project's gate history.
commonMistakes: Mapping phases straight to named people instead of roles.
Phase names in the list that differ from the choice values.
No fallback when a project has no sponsor recorded.
troubleshooting: If the role lookup returns nothing, compare the phase text with the list Title.
If the approver is empty, the project's person column for that role is blank. The coalesce routes it to the PMO.
If a new role is added, extend the Compose_Approver expression with one more branch.

route-approvals-by-risk-severity.shortDescription: Escalate approval to more senior people as the risk rating rises, and require everyone to approve at the top level.
route-approvals-by-risk-severity.fullDescription: Low risks can be accepted by the owner, while high and critical risks need wider sign-off. This pattern maps severity to an approval type and a set of approvers, including a calculated severity from likelihood and impact.
route-approvals-by-risk-severity.problemStatement: All risks go to the same approver, so trivial ones cause delays and serious ones get no more scrutiny than the rest.
whenToUse: Risk acceptance, change approval or exception requests
A defined severity scale
Higher severities needing more than one approver
whenNotToUse: A single approval level
Severity that is not recorded or calculated consistently
route-approvals-by-risk-severity.formulaOrCode:
Compose_Score
  mul(int(triggerBody()?['Likelihood']), int(triggerBody()?['Impact']))      (1 to 25)

Compose_Severity
  if(greaterOrEquals(outputs('Compose_Score'), 15), 'Critical',
  if(greaterOrEquals(outputs('Compose_Score'), 10), 'High',
  if(greaterOrEquals(outputs('Compose_Score'), 5),  'Medium', 'Low')))

Update item   Severity = @{outputs('Compose_Severity')}

Switch on outputs('Compose_Severity')

  Case Low
    Update item Status = Accepted by owner        (no approval)

  Case Medium
    Start and wait for an approval
      Type        : Approve/Reject - First to respond
      Assigned to : @{triggerBody()?['RiskOwner']?['Email']}

  Case High
    Start and wait for an approval
      Type        : Approve/Reject - First to respond
      Assigned to : riskmanager@contoso.com

  Case Critical
    Start and wait for an approval
      Type        : Approve/Reject - Everyone must approve
      Assigned to : riskmanager@contoso.com;ciso@contoso.com;coo@contoso.com

After the Switch
  Update item
    Status : @{if(equals(outputs('Compose_Severity'), 'Low'), 'Accepted', 'Decided')}
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the scale and the thresholds for each severity.
Calculate the score and severity in Compose actions and store the severity on the item.
Switch on severity and start the approval type each level needs.
Use everyone-must-approve for the top level, with addresses separated by semicolons.
Record the decision and who made it.
commonMistakes: Letting the requester choose the severity freely with no calculation.
Using first-to-respond for critical risks.
Leaving thresholds undocumented.
troubleshooting: If int() fails, likelihood or impact is empty. Make both required or wrap them in coalesce.
If an everyone-must-approve approval never finishes, one approver has not responded. Add a timeout and reminder.
If severities look wrong, output the score and check the threshold order from highest to lowest.

route-approvals-by-site-location.shortDescription: Send a request to the approver for its site, with a regional fallback when a site has none.
route-approvals-by-site-location.fullDescription: Multi-site organizations need local approvers. This pattern keeps site approvers in a list with a region column, tries the site first, then the region, then a central mailbox.
route-approvals-by-site-location.problemStatement: Requests from a new or small site stall because the flow has no approver for it, and nobody notices until the requester chases.
whenToUse: Facilities, access or purchasing requests handled per site
Sites grouped into regions
Sites that open and close over time
whenNotToUse: A single location
Approvals by line manager regardless of site
route-approvals-by-site-location.formulaOrCode:
List: Site Approvers
  Title (site code, indexed) | Region (Choice, indexed) | Approver (Person) | IsRegionalLead (Yes/No)

Get items "Site"
  Filter Query : Title eq '@{triggerBody()?['SiteCode']}'
  Top Count    : 1

Get items "Region"
  Filter Query : Region eq '@{triggerBody()?['Region']?['Value']}' and IsRegionalLead eq 1
  Top Count    : 1

Compose_Approver
  coalesce(
    first(body('Site')?['value'])?['Approver']?['Email'],
    first(body('Region')?['value'])?['Approver']?['Email'],
    'facilities@contoso.com'
  )

Compose_RouteUsed   (for reporting gaps)
  if(not(empty(first(body('Site')?['value'])?['Approver']?['Email'])), 'Site',
  if(not(empty(first(body('Region')?['value'])?['Approver']?['Email'])), 'Region', 'Central'))

Update item   RoutedVia = @{outputs('Compose_RouteUsed')}

Start and wait for an approval
  Title       : @{triggerBody()?['SiteCode']}: @{triggerBody()?['Title']}
  Assigned to : @{outputs('Compose_Approver')}
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Site Approvers list with site code, region and approver.
Look up the site, then the regional lead.
Pick the first approver found, ending with a central mailbox.
Record which route was used on the item.
Review items routed centrally each month and fill the gaps in the list.
commonMistakes: No fallback, so unknown sites fail.
Site codes typed by hand on the form instead of chosen from a list.
Never reviewing how often the fallback is used.
troubleshooting: If the site lookup misses, check for leading zeros or different capitals in the code.
If the wrong region lead is chosen, more than one row is marked as lead for that region.
If the central mailbox receives most requests, the list is out of date.

route-approvals-by-vendor-category.shortDescription: Add the right specialist reviews to a vendor request based on what the vendor will supply.
route-approvals-by-vendor-category.fullDescription: A software vendor needs a security review and a contractor needs an insurance check. This pattern stores the required reviews per category and starts only those approvals, in parallel.
route-approvals-by-vendor-category.problemStatement: Every vendor request goes through every review, which wastes specialist time, or reviews are chosen by hand and sometimes skipped.
whenToUse: Vendor, supplier or contract intake
Different categories needing different specialist checks
Reviews that can run at the same time
whenNotToUse: One standard review for all vendors
Categories that overlap so much that every review always applies
stepByStepInstructions: List each category's reviews in the Category Reviews list, with an Any row for reviews everyone needs.
Query the reviews for the request's category.
Loop over them with concurrency on, starting one approval per review.
Write each outcome to a results list.
After the loop, reject the request if any review was rejected.
commonMistakes: Using variables inside the parallel loop to collect outcomes.
Forgetting the reviews that apply to every category.
Running specialist reviews one after another.
troubleshooting: If no reviews start, the category text does not match the list. Compare the values.
If the overall status is wrong, check the results list for that request. Each review should have one row.
If the loop seems stuck, one reviewer has not responded. Add a timeout to the approval action.

route-approvals-by-document-type.shortDescription: Route a document for approval based on its type or content type, and publish it when approved.
route-approvals-by-document-type.fullDescription: Policies, contracts and procedures each have their own approver. This pattern triggers on a library, reads the document type, finds its approver, runs the approval with a link to the file, and sets the approval status.
route-approvals-by-document-type.problemStatement: Documents sit in draft because authors do not know who approves which type, or they email the file around and lose track of versions.
whenToUse: Controlled document libraries
Different owners for different document types
Approval recorded on the file itself
whenNotToUse: Libraries using built-in content approval that already meets the need
Ad hoc files with no type
stepByStepInstructions: Add document type and approval status columns to the library.
Create the Document Approvers list.
Trigger only when the status is set to In review.
Look up the approver for the type and start the approval with a link to the file.
Write the outcome, approver and date to the file's properties.
commonMistakes: Triggering on every modification instead of on the status change.
Approving a link to the library rather than to the specific file.
Not recording which version was approved.
troubleshooting: If the flow runs again after its own update, the trigger condition already stops it because the status is no longer In review. Check the condition text if it loops.
If the file is checked out, the property update fails. Require check-in before review.
If the version shown is not the one reviewed, store the version number in a column at approval time.

route-approvals-by-budget-owner.shortDescription: Find the approver from the cost centre a request is charged to, and check the remaining budget first.
route-approvals-by-budget-owner.fullDescription: The person who should approve spending is the owner of the budget it comes from. This pattern looks up the cost centre, compares the request with the remaining budget, and routes to the budget owner or escalates when the budget would be exceeded.
route-approvals-by-budget-owner.problemStatement: Line managers approve spending against budgets they do not own, and overspends are only found at month end.
whenToUse: Purchase requests charged to cost centres or projects
Budget owners who differ from line managers
A budget figure that is kept up to date somewhere
whenNotToUse: Organizations without cost-centre ownership
Budgets held only in a finance system the flow cannot read
route-approvals-by-budget-owner.formulaOrCode:
List: Cost Centres
  Title (code, indexed) | Owner (Person) | AnnualBudget (Currency) | Committed (Currency) | FinancePartner (Person)

Get items (Cost Centres)
  Filter Query : Title eq '@{triggerBody()?['CostCentre']}'
  Top Count    : 1

Condition: length(body('Get_items')?['value']) is equal to 0
  Yes: Update item Status = Needs attention, FlowMessage = Unknown cost centre
       Terminate (Failed, "UnknownCostCentre")

Compose_Remaining
  sub(
    float(coalesce(first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['AnnualBudget'], 0)),
    float(coalesce(first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['Committed'], 0))
  )

Compose_OverBudget
  greater(float(triggerBody()?['Amount']), outputs('Compose_Remaining'))

Condition: outputs('Compose_OverBudget') is equal to true
  No : Start and wait for an approval (First to respond)
         Assigned to : budget owner
         Details     : Remaining budget: @{formatNumber(outputs('Compose_Remaining'), 'N2')}
  Yes: Start and wait for an approval (Everyone must approve)
         Assigned to : budget owner;finance partner
         Details     : **This request exceeds the remaining budget of
                       @{formatNumber(outputs('Compose_Remaining'), 'N2')}.**

On approval: Update item (Cost Centres)  Committed = Committed + Amount
stepByStepInstructions: Keep a Cost Centres list with owner, budget and committed spend.
Look up the request's cost centre and stop clearly when it is unknown.
Calculate the remaining budget and whether the request exceeds it.
Route to the owner, adding the finance partner when the budget would be exceeded.
Add the amount to committed spend when the request is approved.
commonMistakes: Routing to the line manager when someone else owns the budget.
Not updating committed spend, so the remaining figure is always the full budget.
Trying to set the approval type with an expression. Use a Condition with two approval actions.
troubleshooting: If remaining budget is wrong, two approvals updated Committed at the same time. Re-read the row just before updating it.
If float() fails, a currency column is empty. Keep the coalesce defaults.
If the owner is the requester, route to the finance partner instead.

route-approvals-by-change-impact.shortDescription: Classify a change as standard, normal or major from a few questions and route it accordingly.
route-approvals-by-change-impact.fullDescription: Change requests should not all go to a review board. This pattern scores impact from yes/no answers, auto-approves standard changes, sends normal ones to the service owner, and sends major ones to a board with everyone required to approve.
route-approvals-by-change-impact.problemStatement: Low-risk routine changes wait a week for the change board, while the board's agenda is too full to examine the risky ones properly.
whenToUse: IT or process change management
A change form with clear risk questions
A pre-approved list of standard changes
whenNotToUse: Emergency changes, which need their own fast path
Teams without an agreed definition of impact
stepByStepInstructions: Add the yes/no impact questions to the change form.
Score the answers and classify the change in two Compose actions.
Store the impact and score on the item so the decision can be explained.
Switch on impact: approve standard changes, route normal and major ones.
Notify the requester and service desk of the outcome.
commonMistakes: Letting requesters pick the impact level directly.
Auto-approving anything marked standard without a score check.
Not storing the score, so nobody can see why a change was classified as it was.
troubleshooting: If every change scores as major, check that a missing rollback plan is not being counted twice.
If yes/no values arrive as text, compare with equals(..., true) inside the if.
If the board approval stalls, set a timeout matched to the board's meeting cycle.

route-approvals-by-support-team.shortDescription: Assign a request to the right support team's queue and ask that team's lead to approve.
route-approvals-by-support-team.fullDescription: Service requests need both an owner team and an approver. This pattern maps the request's service to a team, sets the team on the item so it appears in that team's view, posts to the team's channel, and asks the lead for approval when the service requires one.
route-approvals-by-support-team.problemStatement: Requests land in one shared queue, and a coordinator spends the day forwarding them to the right team.
whenToUse: Service desks with several fulfilment teams
Services that map cleanly to a team
Some services needing approval and others not
whenNotToUse: One team handling everything
Requests that need triage by a person before they can be assigned
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Services list with team, lead and approval flag.
Look up the request's service and set the team on the item.
Start an approval only when the service needs one.
Post queued requests to the team's channel using IDs stored in the list.
Create a view per team filtered by AssignedTeam.
commonMistakes: Approving everything, including services that need no approval.
Hard-coding Teams channel IDs in the flow.
No triage route for unmapped services.
troubleshooting: If the Teams post fails, the stored group or channel ID is wrong. Copy them from the channel's link.
If requests end up in Triage, the service is missing from the list.
If the lead is away, add a deputy column and a timeout that reassigns.

send-reminder-emails-for-pending-approva.shortDescription: Remind approvers about approvals that are still waiting, without changing the original approval flow.
send-reminder-emails-for-pending-approva.fullDescription: A separate scheduled flow reads requests that have been awaiting approval for too long and reminds each approver once a day with all of their pending items. It relies on the approval flow stamping the approver and request date on the item.
send-reminder-emails-for-pending-approva.problemStatement: Approvals sit unanswered for days, and the only reminder is the requester chasing by chat.
whenToUse: Approvals that regularly wait more than a day or two
Flows where the approver is recorded on the item
Reminders that should group all pending items per approver
whenNotToUse: Approvals with a built-in timeout and escalation already in the same flow
Items with no recorded approver
send-reminder-emails-for-pending-approva.formulaOrCode:
In the approval flow, before Start and wait for an approval: Update item Status : Awaiting approval PendingApprover : ApprovalRequested : @{utcNow()} Reminder flow Trigger: Recurrence (weekdays 09:00) Get items Filter Query : Status eq 'Awaiting approval' and ApprovalRequested lt '@{addDays(utcNow(), -2)}' Select_Approvers (text mode) @toLower(item()?['PendingApprover']?['Email']) Compose_Distinct union(body('Select_Approvers'), body('Select_Approvers')) Apply to each approver Filter array @equals(toLower(item()?['PendingApprover']?['Email']), items('Apply_to_each')) Select Request -> item()?['Title'] Requester -> item()?['Author']?['DisplayName'] Waiting -> concat(string(div(sub(ticks(utcNow()), ticks(item()?['ApprovalRequested'])), 864000000000)), ' days') Create HTML table Send an email (V2) To : @{items('Apply_to_each')} Subject : @{length(body('Filter_array'))} approvals are waiting for you Body : @{body('Create_HTML_table')}

Respond in the Approvals app in Teams or from the original email.
stepByStepInstructions: Stamp the approver and request time on the item in the approval flow.
Build a scheduled flow that reads items waiting longer than your limit.
Group by approver with Select, union and Filter array.
Send each approver one email listing their pending items and how long each has waited.
Clear the pending columns in the approval flow when a decision is made.
commonMistakes: Building the reminder as a delay loop inside the approval flow, which is hard to change.
One reminder email per item.
Not clearing the pending marker after the decision.
troubleshooting: If people are reminded about approvals they already answered, the approval flow is not updating the status after the response.
If no reminders go out, check the date filter format and that ApprovalRequested is indexed on large lists.
If the Teams link does not open the Approvals app, link to the item instead.

send-escalation-emails-for-rejected-requ.shortDescription: Tell the requester why a request was rejected, and give them one clear way to appeal or resubmit.
send-escalation-emails-for-rejected-requ.fullDescription: A rejection with no reason generates follow-up work. This pattern sends the approver's comments to the requester, offers resubmit and appeal links, and escalates to a second reviewer only when an appeal is raised.
send-escalation-emails-for-rejected-requ.problemStatement: Requesters get a bare rejection, reply to the wrong person asking why, and submit the same request again unchanged.
whenToUse: Any approval where rejection needs explaining
Processes with a right of appeal
Requests that are often fixed and resubmitted
whenNotToUse: Final decisions with no appeal
Rejections that must be delivered by a person
send-escalation-emails-for-rejected-requ.formulaOrCode:
After the approval, in the Rejected branch: Compose_Reason coalesce(first(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses'])?['comments'], 'No reason was given.') Update item Status : Rejected DecisionNote : @{outputs('Compose_Reason')} RejectedBy : Send email with options To : @{triggerBody()?['Author']?['Email']} Subject : Your request was not approved: @{triggerBody()?['Title']} Options : Edit and resubmit, Appeal this decision, Accept Body :

@{first(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses'])?['responder']?['displayName']} did not approve this request.

Reason: @{outputs('Compose_Reason')}

(Settings: Timeout P14D) Switch on body('Send_email_with_options')?['SelectedOption'] Edit and resubmit Update item Status = Draft Send an email with the edit link: @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']} Appeal this decision Update item Status = Under appeal Start and wait for an approval Assigned to : appeals@contoso.com Details : Original decision by : @{outputs('Compose_Reason')} Update item Status = Approved on appeal | Rejected on appeal Accept (or timeout) Update item Status = Closed
stepByStepInstructions: Capture the approver's comments and store them on the item.
Email the requester the reason with three options.
Reset the item to draft when they choose to edit and resubmit.
Route appeals to a second reviewer with the original reason attached.
Close the item when the requester accepts or does not respond in time.
commonMistakes: Sending a rejection with no reason.
Routing appeals back to the same approver.
