whenNotToUse: Standard edit forms, where the data card's Required property and SubmitForm do this
Rules that must also apply to edits made outside the app, which belong in SharePoint column validation as well
stepByStepInstructions: List every rule as a row with a field name, a failing condition and a message.
Collect only the failed rows when the user presses Save.
If nothing failed, run the Patch inside IfError.
Otherwise show the messages in a gallery near the button.
Set each input's border colour from the error collection.
commonMistakes: Checking only IsBlank and letting whitespace through. Trim first.
Disabling the Save button with no explanation of what is missing.
Validating in the app only, when the list can also be edited directly.
troubleshooting: If a rule never fires, test its condition in a label to see the value it returns.
If the border colour does not reset, clear the collection when the screen becomes visible.
If SharePoint still rejects the save, the list has a required column or validation rule the app does not cover. FirstError.Message names it.
If a combo box is treated as filled when empty, check IsEmpty(cmb.SelectedItems) instead of IsBlank.

build-a-confirmation-dialog-before-destr.shortDescription: Show an are-you-sure dialog before delete, cancel or reset, and run the action only on confirm.
build-a-confirmation-dialog-before-destr.fullDescription: Destructive buttons should not act on the first tap. This pattern stores the pending action in a variable, shows an overlay with confirm and cancel buttons, and runs the action from the confirm button.
build-a-confirmation-dialog-before-destr.problemStatement: Users delete records by accident and there is no undo.
whenToUse: Delete, cancel, reject and reset actions
Bulk actions on selected rows
Any action that cannot be undone
whenNotToUse: Routine saves, where a dialog only slows people down
Actions that can be undone, where an undo message is friendlier
stepByStepInstructions: Add a container with a dimmed background, a title, a message and two buttons.
Set the container's Visible to a context variable.
On the destructive icon, store the action name, the message and the record in the variable.
Run the real action from the Confirm button and clear the variable afterwards.
Name the item in the message so the user can see what will be affected.
commonMistakes: Running the delete from the first button and showing the dialog afterwards.
A generic message that does not say what will be deleted.
Leaving controls behind the dialog tappable.
troubleshooting: If the dialog appears behind other controls, bring its container to the front in the tree view.
If the wrong record is deleted, the gallery selection changed. Use the record stored in the variable, not the gallery's Selected.
If Remove fails, the user may lack delete permission. The error message from FirstError says so.
If the dialog does not close after an error, move the UpdateContext outside the IfError as shown.

create-a-reusable-loading-overlay.shortDescription: Show a full-screen spinner while a save, load or flow call is running, and block double taps.
create-a-reusable-loading-overlay.fullDescription: A loading overlay tells the user something is happening and stops them pressing the button twice. This pattern uses one variable and one container, with an optional message.
create-a-reusable-loading-overlay.problemStatement: Users press Save repeatedly because nothing appears to happen, which creates duplicate records.
whenToUse: Patch, SubmitForm and flow calls that take more than a moment
Screens that load data when they open
Any action where a second tap would cause harm
whenNotToUse: Very fast actions, where a flash of overlay is distracting
Background refreshes the user does not need to wait for
stepByStepInstructions: Add a container that covers the screen, with a semi-transparent fill and a spinner.
Bind its Visible property to a busy variable.
Set the variable to true before the slow action and false after it, including on failure.
Disable the trigger button while busy.
For app-wide use, move the overlay into a component driven by a global variable.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to turn the overlay off when the action fails, which locks the screen.
Placing the overlay below other controls in the tree, so it does not cover them.
Using a timer to hide the overlay instead of the action's completion.
troubleshooting: If the overlay never shows, the action is faster than a screen refresh, which is fine.
If the overlay stays on, an error skipped the line that hides it. Wrap the action in IfError and hide the overlay after it.
If SubmitForm never hides it, add the reset to both OnSuccess and OnFailure.
If the spinner image does not animate, use the modern Spinner control or an animated GIF or SVG.

use-named-formulas-for-app-constants.shortDescription: Define colours, list names, role checks and other fixed values once in App.Formulas instead of setting variables in OnStart.
use-named-formulas-for-app-constants.fullDescription: Named formulas are defined in the App object's Formulas property. They are calculated when needed, always up to date and cannot be changed by accident, which makes them a better home for constants than global variables.
use-named-formulas-for-app-constants.problemStatement: App.OnStart is full of Set calls for colours and settings, which slows start-up and lets any screen overwrite them.
whenToUse: Theme colours, sizes and text used on many screens
Values derived from the current user, such as role checks
Lookups of settings that rarely change
whenNotToUse: Values that the app changes while running. Those need Set or UpdateContext.
Formulas with side effects such as Patch or Collect, which named formulas cannot contain
stepByStepInstructions: Select the App object and open its Formulas property.
Move constants out of OnStart and define each as Name = expression followed by a semicolon.
Group related values in a record, such as a theme.
Replace references to the old global variables across the app.
Keep OnStart for actions only, such as loading collections.
commonMistakes: Trying to Set a named formula. They are read-only by design.
Putting behaviour functions such as Collect or Navigate in a formula.
Leaving the old variable in OnStart with the same name, which causes a naming conflict.
troubleshooting: If the editor reports an unexpected character, a semicolon is missing between definitions. In regions that use a comma as the decimal separator, definitions end with a double semicolon.
If a value does not refresh, call Refresh on its data source. Named formulas recalculate when their inputs change.
If a circular reference is reported, two formulas depend on each other. Break the loop.
If the app is slow on first use of a screen, a named formula that calls a connector is being evaluated then. That is expected and happens once.

cache-reference-data-on-app-start.shortDescription: Load small, rarely changing lists into collections once so dropdowns and lookups respond instantly.
cache-reference-data-on-app-start.fullDescription: Reference data such as departments, categories and settings is read constantly and changes rarely. Loading it once into collections, in parallel, cuts connector calls and removes delegation limits on small lists.
cache-reference-data-on-app-start.problemStatement: Every dropdown and LookUp calls SharePoint again, so screens load slowly and the app makes hundreds of requests per session.
whenToUse: Lists of up to a few hundred rows that change rarely
Data used on several screens
LookUps repeated inside galleries
whenNotToUse: Transactional lists that change during the session
Lists larger than the data row limit, which would be cut off silently
stepByStepInstructions: Identify the small lists the app reads repeatedly.
Load them into collections inside Concurrent so the calls run in parallel.
Keep only the columns you need with ShowColumns.
Point dropdowns and lookups at the collections.
Add a refresh button and warn if a list reaches the row limit.
commonMistakes: Caching a list larger than the data row limit, which loads only the first 500 or 2,000 rows.
Caching data that users change during the session.
Loading every column, including ones never used.
troubleshooting: If a dropdown is missing entries, the list has more rows than the data row limit. Filter it or raise the limit in Settings, up to 2,000.
If a new item does not appear, the cache is stale. Use the refresh button.
If start-up is still slow, check for calls outside Concurrent and for large lists being loaded.
If a choice or lookup default does not match after caching, compare on ID rather than on the whole record.

reset-form-controls-after-cancel.shortDescription: Discard unsaved input and return every control to its starting value when the user cancels.
reset-form-controls-after-cancel.fullDescription: An edit form resets with ResetForm. A custom form built from individual inputs needs each control reset, which is done with Reset or by toggling a variable bound to each control's Reset property.
reset-form-controls-after-cancel.problemStatement: A user cancels, reopens the form and sees the values they typed last time, or a new form opens showing the previous record's data.
whenToUse: Cancel and close buttons
Forms reused for new and edit
Dialogs that open more than once per session
whenNotToUse: Forms that should keep a draft between visits
Screens that are rebuilt each time from a fresh variable
stepByStepInstructions: Give every input a Default that reads from the record variable.
For an edit form, call ResetForm on cancel.
For a custom form, bind each control's Reset property to one variable and toggle it true then false.
Clear related state such as validation errors.
When opening a blank form, clear the record variable before resetting.
commonMistakes: Calling Reset on a control with no Default, which just empties it.
Using two separate behaviours for new and edit that drift apart.
Forgetting collections and variables that hold form state.
troubleshooting: If a combo box keeps its selection, check DefaultSelectedItems is a table and toggle the reset after changing the record variable.
If Reset is not accepted for a control, it may be inside a gallery or component. Use the Reset property with a variable instead.
If the previous record's values flash on open, set the record variable before making the form visible.
If ResetForm does not clear a new form, call NewForm again after it.

use-a-context-variable-for-screen-level-.shortDescription: Keep whether a screen is in view or edit mode in a context variable and drive every control from it.
use-a-context-variable-for-screen-level-.fullDescription: A single context variable for the screen's mode keeps the logic in one place. Controls read it to decide their display mode, buttons switch it, and it resets naturally each time the screen opens.
use-a-context-variable-for-screen-level-.problemStatement: Edit state is scattered across global variables, so one screen's mode leaks into another and controls disagree about whether editing is allowed.
whenToUse: Detail screens that switch between view and edit
State that belongs to one screen
Screens opened from several places with different starting modes
whenNotToUse: State needed by other screens, which belongs in a global variable or collection
Standard edit forms where FormMode already does the job
stepByStepInstructions: Pass the starting mode and the record as the third argument of Navigate.
Set each input's DisplayMode from the mode variable.
Show Edit, Save and Cancel buttons according to the mode.
Switch modes with UpdateContext, and store the result of Patch back into the record variable.
Avoid setting the same state in global variables.
commonMistakes: Using a global variable, so a mode set on one screen affects another.
Storing several booleans such as isEdit and isNew that can contradict each other.
Not updating the record variable after saving, so the screen shows old values.
troubleshooting: If the variable is blank when the screen opens, a Navigate call elsewhere omits the context record. Set a default in OnVisible with If(IsBlank(locMode), UpdateContext({ locMode: "View" })).
If controls stay editable, check their DisplayMode is not also set by a parent container.
If the mode persists from the last visit, context variables keep their value. Always pass the mode in Navigate.
If the form ignores the mode, an explicit EditForm or NewForm call elsewhere is overriding DefaultMode.

create-a-reusable-notification-pattern.shortDescription: Standardise success, warning and error messages with one helper so every screen reports results the same way.
create-a-reusable-notification-pattern.fullDescription: Notify works, but calls scattered through an app end up with inconsistent wording, timing and types. This pattern centralises messages, shows friendly text for known errors and logs the technical detail.
create-a-reusable-notification-pattern.problemStatement: Users see raw connector errors on one screen, nothing on another, and success messages that vanish before they can be read.
whenToUse: Apps with many save and submit actions
Teams building several apps that should behave alike
Errors that need a friendly explanation
whenNotToUse: A single-screen app with one or two messages
Messages that need buttons or links, which need a custom banner instead
stepByStepInstructions: Put standard message texts in a named formula.
Add a function or shared formula that maps technical errors to friendly text.
Wrap data actions in IfError and call Notify with consistent types and durations.
Handle anything missed in App.OnError.
Send technical details to Trace so they appear in Monitor and Application Insights.
commonMistakes: Showing FirstError.Message directly to users.
Using the default timeout for errors, which is too short to read.
Reporting success before the action has finished.
troubleshooting: If user-defined functions are not available, enable them in Settings, or use a named formula record and an inline If.
If two messages appear, both the local IfError and App.OnError are handling the same error. Errors handled by IfError do not reach OnError unless re-raised.
If Trace output is missing, connect the app to Application Insights or open Monitor while testing.
If a notification is hidden behind the app header in Teams, use a custom banner label instead of Notify.

filter-galleries-by-current-user.shortDescription: Show each user only their own records with a delegable filter on a SharePoint person column.
filter-galleries-by-current-user.fullDescription: Filtering on a person column's Email is delegable in SharePoint, as long as the user's email is captured in a variable first. This pattern covers created-by, assigned-to and multi-person cases.
filter-galleries-by-current-user.problemStatement: The filter works in testing and then shows a delegation warning, or misses records once the list passes 2,000 items.
whenToUse: My items, my tasks and my approvals views
Lists with a person column or the built-in Created By
Lists that will grow beyond the data row limit
whenNotToUse: Security. A filter hides rows but does not protect them. Use item permissions for that.
Multi-person columns on large lists, which cannot be filtered server-side
stepByStepInstructions: Store the user's email in a variable or named formula.
Filter on the person column's Email property using that variable.
Add other delegable conditions such as status and StartsWith.
For multi-person columns, reduce the set with a delegable filter first.
On very large lists, add an indexed text column that holds the owner's email.
commonMistakes: Calling User().Email inside the Filter, which can block delegation and repeats the call.
Comparing DisplayName, which is not unique.
Treating a filtered gallery as security.
troubleshooting: If no rows match, the stored email and the sign-in name differ, which happens for guests and after a rename. Compare both values in a label, and try the Claims value instead.
If a delegation warning remains, look for in, Lower on the column, or a multi-person column in the filter.
If the list has more than 5,000 items and the filter fails, index the column or use the text column approach.
If case differences cause misses, lower-case the variable. SharePoint compares the email without regard to case.

build-a-my-requests-view.shortDescription: Build a screen where requesters see their own submissions, with status tabs, search and counts.
build-a-my-requests-view.fullDescription: A My Requests screen answers the question every requester asks: where is my request? This pattern builds it with a delegable filter, status tabs, a status pill and a useful empty state.
build-a-my-requests-view.problemStatement: Requesters email the team for updates because the app has no simple view of what they submitted and where it stands.
whenToUse: Request, ticket and approval apps
Apps where requesters and processors use different screens
Lists with a status column
whenNotToUse: Apps where every user works every record
Lists with no status to report
build-a-my-requests-view.formulaOrCode:
// Tabs (horizontal gallery) Items
["Open", "Completed", "All"]
// OnSelect : UpdateContext({ locTab: ThisItem.Value })     Screen.OnVisible : UpdateContext({ locTab: "Open" })

// Main gallery Items (all delegable)
SortByColumns(
    Filter(
        Requests,
        Author.Email = gblUserEmail,
        locTab = "All"
            || (locTab = "Open"      && Status.Value <> "Completed" && Status.Value <> "Rejected" && Status.Value <> "Cancelled")
            || (locTab = "Completed" && (Status.Value = "Completed" || Status.Value = "Rejected" || Status.Value = "Cancelled")),
        StartsWith(Title, txtSearch.Text)
    ),
    "Created", SortOrder.Descending
)

// Row content
lblTitle.Text  : ThisItem.Title
lblMeta.Text   : "Submitted " & Text(ThisItem.Created, "d mmm yyyy") &
                 If(!IsBlank(ThisItem.AssignedTo), " · With " & ThisItem.AssignedTo.DisplayName)
lblStatus.Text : ThisItem.Status.Value
lblStatus.Fill : Switch(ThisItem.Status.Value,
                    "Approved",  RGBA(223, 246, 221, 1),
                    "Completed", RGBA(223, 246, 221, 1),
                    "Rejected",  RGBA(253, 231, 233, 1),
                    "In review", RGBA(255, 244, 206, 1),
                    RGBA(243, 242, 241, 1))

// Empty state label
Visible : IsEmpty(galMyRequests.AllItems)
Text    : If(IsBlank(txtSearch.Text),
             "You have no " & Lower(locTab) & " requests.",
             "Nothing matches "" & txtSearch.Text & "".")

// Open a request
galMyRequests.OnSelect : Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.None, { locRecord: ThisItem, locMode: "View" })

// New request button always visible on this screen
stepByStepInstructions: Capture the user's email in a variable.
Add tabs for open, completed and all, stored in a context variable.
Filter the list by author, tab and search text, sorted newest first.
Show the status as a coloured pill with the date and current assignee.
Add an empty state and a button to start a new request.
commonMistakes: Showing every status in one long list with no way to narrow it.
Using CountRows on the data source for tab counts, which is not delegable on large lists.
No message when the list is empty, so users think the app is broken.
troubleshooting: If a delegation warning appears, check the tab logic uses only equals and not-equals on the status value.
If requests submitted on someone's behalf are missing, filter on a Requester person column instead of Author.
If new requests do not appear after submitting, call Refresh(Requests) when returning to this screen.
If counts are needed on tabs, collect the user's requests once and count the collection.

create-an-admin-only-maintenance-screen.shortDescription: Add a screen for app administrators to fix data and manage settings, hidden from everyone else.
create-an-admin-only-maintenance-screen.fullDescription: Every app needs somewhere to correct stuck records and edit reference data without opening SharePoint. This pattern checks admin membership once, hides the entry point and guards the screen itself.
create-an-admin-only-maintenance-screen.problemStatement: Fixing a stuck request means editing the list directly, which bypasses the app's rules and is easy to get wrong.
whenToUse: Apps with reference data or settings that change
Records that occasionally need manual correction
A small, known group of administrators
whenNotToUse: As the only protection for sensitive data. Hiding a screen is not security.
Apps where admins already work comfortably in the list
stepByStepInstructions: Decide where admin membership is kept: a list or a group.
Evaluate it once in a named formula.
Show the admin entry point only to admins, and redirect non-admins in the screen's OnVisible.
Add tools for finding a record, correcting its status with a reason, and editing reference data.
Write every admin change to a log list.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding admin email addresses in formulas.
Hiding the button but not guarding the screen.
Assuming the screen protects data. Users with list access can still edit the list directly.
troubleshooting: If an admin cannot see the icon, compare their email with the list entry, including case and guest formats.
If the group check is slow or fails, the user may lack permission to read group members. Use the list approach.
If non-admins can still change data, restrict permissions on the list itself, or route changes through a flow.
If the admin list hits a delegation warning, it is small enough to ignore, or filter with StartsWith on the title.

use-a-sharepoint-settings-list-for-app-c.shortDescription: Keep thresholds, email addresses, messages and switches in a SharePoint list so they can change without republishing the app.
use-a-sharepoint-settings-list-for-app-c.fullDescription: A key and value settings list moves configuration out of formulas. The app loads it once, reads typed values through small helpers, and falls back to defaults when a setting is missing.
use-a-sharepoint-settings-list-for-app-c.problemStatement: Changing an approval threshold or support address means editing the app, testing and republishing.
whenToUse: Values the business changes from time to time
Different values per environment
Feature switches and banner messages
whenNotToUse: Secrets such as keys and passwords, which do not belong in a list
Values that never change. A named formula is simpler.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the settings list with a unique key, a value and a description.
Give most users read access and only administrators edit access.
Load the list into a collection at start.
Expose each setting through a named formula that converts the type and supplies a default.
Use the same list from flows so the app and flows agree.
commonMistakes: No default, so a missing row breaks the app.
Reading the list with a new LookUp against SharePoint in every formula.
Storing secrets or connection details in the list.
troubleshooting: If a setting change does not show, the app loaded settings at start. Restart the app or add a refresh button.
If Value() errors, the setting holds text that is not a number. The Coalesce default only covers blank.
If users cannot load settings, they lack read access to the list.
If named formulas show a blank on first load, the collection is still loading. Reference the list directly in the named formula instead of the collection.

build-a-reusable-approval-comments-panel.shortDescription: Build one comments dialog that approve, reject and send-back buttons all share, with a required reason where needed.
build-a-reusable-approval-comments-panel.fullDescription: Approval actions differ only in the status they set and whether a comment is required. This pattern uses one overlay configured by a variable, saves the decision with who and when, and appends the comment to a history column.
build-a-reusable-approval-comments-panel.problemStatement: Each approval button has its own copy of the dialog and save logic, and rejections are saved with no reason.
whenToUse: Screens with approve, reject and return actions
Decisions that need a comment
Apps that keep a comment history on the item
whenNotToUse: Approvals handled entirely in Power Automate or Teams
One-click approvals with no comment
stepByStepInstructions: Build one overlay with a title, a multi-line text input and confirm and cancel buttons.
From each action button, set a record variable describing the action, target status and whether a comment is required.
Disable confirm until a required comment is long enough.
Patch the status, comment, approver and time, and add a line to the history column.
Reset the input and hide the panel.
commonMistakes: Three near-identical dialogs that drift apart.
Allowing a rejection with no reason.
Overwriting the previous comment so earlier decisions are lost.
troubleshooting:
If the history shows on one line, the column is plain text displayed in a single-line label. Use a multi-line label or HTML text with Substitute(history, Char(10), "
").
If two approvers act at once, the later save wins. Re-read the item in the LookUp as shown and check its status is still pending before patching.
If the comment box keeps old text, reset it on both confirm and cancel.
If the comment is cut off, the column is single line of text, which holds 255 characters. Use multiple lines.

track-unsaved-changes-before-navigation.shortDescription: Detect edits that have not been saved and ask the user before they leave the screen.
track-unsaved-changes-before-navigation.fullDescription: Power Apps does not warn about unsaved work. This pattern detects changes, using the form's Unsaved property or a comparison for custom forms, and routes every exit through one check that shows a discard dialog.
track-unsaved-changes-before-navigation.problemStatement: Users press Back, tap a menu item or close a dialog and lose everything they typed, with no warning.
whenToUse: Long forms
Screens with several ways to leave
Custom forms built from individual controls
whenNotToUse: Short forms that save automatically
Read-only screens
stepByStepInstructions: Decide how to detect changes: the form's Unsaved property, or a comparison of inputs with the record.
Send every way of leaving the screen through one check.
If there are changes, show a dialog with keep editing, discard, and save and leave.
On discard, reset the form before navigating.
Show a small unsaved indicator so users know the state.
commonMistakes: Guarding the Back icon but not the menu or other navigation.
Setting a dirty flag in OnChange, which also fires when defaults load.
Not resetting the form on discard, so the edits reappear later.
troubleshooting: If Unsaved is true as soon as the form opens, a data card's Default differs from the stored value, often a date or a trimmed text. Fix the default.
If the comparison is always true for a blank field, wrap both sides in Coalesce.
Closing the browser tab or the mobile app cannot be intercepted from a canvas app. For long forms, add a draft save.
If Select reports that it cannot be used, the target button must be on the same screen.

create-dependent-checklist-rows-from-a-t.shortDescription: Copy a set of template rows into a child list for a new parent record, in one bulk Patch.
create-dependent-checklist-rows-from-a-t.fullDescription: When a project, onboarding or audit is created, it usually needs the same starting checklist. This pattern reads template rows, builds the child rows in memory with the parent's ID, and writes them in a single Patch call.
create-dependent-checklist-rows-from-a-t.problemStatement: Each new record needs ten standard checklist items, and creating them one at a time with ForAll is slow and sometimes stops partway.
whenToUse: Parent records that start with a standard set of child rows
Templates that vary by type
Up to a few hundred rows per parent
whenNotToUse: Very large sets, where a flow is more reliable
Child rows that must be created even if the user closes the app. Use a flow triggered by the parent.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a template list and a child list with an indexed ParentId number column.
Patch the parent first and store the returned record to get its ID.
Use ForAll to shape the template rows into new child records in a collection.
Write the collection with a single Patch call.
Check that no child rows exist before creating them again.
commonMistakes: Calling Patch inside ForAll once per row, which is much slower.
Reading the parent ID from the form instead of from the result of Patch.
Using a lookup column for the parent, which makes bulk Patch more awkward than a number column.
troubleshooting: If the bulk Patch reports a type mismatch, the collection's column names or types differ from the list. Choice columns need a record with Value.
If only some rows are created, the app was closed mid-save or throttled. Compare counts and offer a retry for the missing rows.
If the template filter shows a delegation warning, the template list is small, so it is safe, or cache it in a collection first.
If rows are created twice, add the existence check and disable the button while saving.

use-concat-to-summarize-selected-rows.shortDescription: Turn selected rows or a table of values into one readable string for labels, emails and text columns.
use-concat-to-summarize-selected-rows.fullDescription: Concat joins a value from every row of a table with a separator. This pattern covers gallery selections, combo boxes, multi-choice columns, tidy separators and totals alongside the text.
use-concat-to-summarize-selected-rows.problemStatement: A label or email needs a list of the selected items, but binding it to a table shows nothing or [object Object].
whenToUse: Summaries of checked gallery rows
Displaying multi-select choices or people
Building text for an email or a notes column
whenNotToUse: Long lists, which read better in a gallery or HTML table
Data that needs to stay structured for later filtering
stepByStepInstructions: Collect the selected rows, or use the control's SelectedItems.
Call Concat with the table, the value to take from each row and a separator.
Format each value inside the second argument where needed.
Handle the empty and single-item cases for readable text.
Use the result in a label, an email body or a text column.
commonMistakes: Passing a table straight to a label's Text.
Adding the separator inside the expression and ending up with a trailing comma. Use the third argument.
Saving a summary to a single-line column that is limited to 255 characters.
troubleshooting: If the result is blank, the field name in the second argument does not exist on the table. Check with the formula bar's suggestions.

If line breaks do not show, the label is single line. Turn off auto height limits or use an HTML text control with
.
If the checkbox state is lost when scrolling, bind its Default to the collection as shown.
If values repeat, wrap the table in Distinct.

build-a-compact-power-apps-audit-note.shortDescription: Record who changed what and when from the app itself, as a line on the item or a row in a history list.
build-a-compact-power-apps-audit-note.fullDescription: SharePoint version history exists but is awkward to read from an app. This pattern builds a short note from the changed fields at save time and writes it either to an append-style text column or to a separate history list.
build-a-compact-power-apps-audit-note.problemStatement: When a record looks wrong, nobody can tell from the app who changed the status or the owner, or why.
whenToUse: Status, owner and priority changes that need explaining later
Apps where users should see recent activity on a record
Light audit needs without a flow
whenNotToUse: Formal audit requirements, which need server-side logging that users cannot bypass
Lists edited outside the app, where app-side notes miss changes
stepByStepInstructions: List the fields worth auditing with their old and new values.
Keep only the rows where the value changed and join them into one line.
Skip the save if nothing changed.
Write the line to a notes column, a history list, or both.
Show the latest entries on the record's detail screen.
commonMistakes: Logging every save even when nothing changed.
Comparing whole choice or person records instead of their values.
Letting the notes column grow without limit.
troubleshooting: If every save reports a change, a comparison is between different types, such as a date and text. Format both sides the same way.
If notes are cut off, the column is single line. Use multiple lines of plain text.
If the history list filter shows a delegation warning, make RequestId a number column and index it.
If edits made directly in SharePoint are missing from the log, that is expected. Use a flow on the list for complete coverage.

create-a-power-apps-formula-pack-outline.shortDescription: Organise the formulas a team reuses into a documented pack, with naming rules and a tested example for each.
create-a-power-apps-formula-pack-outline.fullDescription: A formula pack is a shared, versioned set of the Power Fx snippets a team copies between apps. This pattern gives a structure for it: what to include, how to document each formula, and where to keep it so it stays current.
create-a-power-apps-formula-pack-outline.problemStatement: Each maker keeps their own notes of useful formulas, so the same problem is solved five different ways across the team's apps.
whenToUse: Teams with more than one maker
Organisations building several similar apps
Onboarding new makers
whenNotToUse: A single maker with one app
Logic that belongs in a component library, which is reusable without copying
create-a-power-apps-formula-pack-outline.formulaOrCode:
Formula pack structure (one page or list item per formula)

  Name          : Patch a person column
  Category      : Patch | Filter | Dates | Collections | Navigation | Error handling | Text
  Use when      : Saving a single user to a SharePoint person column
  Depends on    : SharePoint list with a Person column "AssignedTo"; Office 365 Users connector
  Formula       : (below, with generic control names)
  Replace       : Requests, AssignedTo, cmbPerson
  Known limits  : Guests need the Claims format shown
  Tested on     : date, app version, tester
  Owner         : maker's name

Example entry
  Patch(
      Requests,
      varRecord,
      {
          AssignedTo: {
              '@odata.type': "#Microsoft.Azure.Connectors.SharePoint.SPListExpandedUser",
              Claims: "i:0#.f|membership|" & Lower(cmbPerson.Selected.Mail),
              DisplayName: cmbPerson.Selected.DisplayName,
              Email: cmbPerson.Selected.Mail,
              Department: "", JobTitle: "", Picture: ""
          }
      }
  )

Suggested starting set (about 25 formulas)
  Patch        : choice, multi-choice, person, lookup, date and time, yes/no, clear a field
  Filter       : by current user, date range, StartsWith search, status tabs
  Collections  : cache reference data, bulk Patch, remove duplicates, group and sum
  Dates        : working days between dates, start of week, age in days
  Errors       : IfError around Patch, App.OnError handler, friendly messages
  Navigation   : deep link with Param, pass a record, confirm before leaving
  Text         : initials, proper case, join selected values

Naming rules to include
  Controls   : txt, dd, cmb, dp, gal, btn, lbl, ico, frm, con + purpose (txtTitle)
  Variables  : gbl (global), loc (context), col (collection), nf (named formula)

Where to keep it
  A SharePoint list or wiki page for reading, plus a component library or a "starter" app
  in a shared environment for the pieces that can be reused without copying.
stepByStepInstructions: Collect the formulas your team already copies between apps.
Write each one up in the same format: when to use it, the formula, what to replace and known limits.
Agree naming rules and apply them to every example.
Store the pack where makers will find it, and give each entry an owner.
Review it twice a year and after major Power Apps releases.
commonMistakes: A long document of snippets with no explanation of when each applies.
Examples that use one app's real names, so they need heavy editing.
No owner, so entries go out of date.
troubleshooting: If makers do not use the pack, it is hard to search. Put it in a list with a category column and a search box.
If examples fail when pasted, they depend on a connector or column that was not listed. Add a Depends on line.
If two entries solve the same problem, pick one and retire the other.
If formulas need frequent changes, move that logic into a component or a user-defined function instead.

patch-sharepoint-rich-text-notes-from-po.shortDescription: Save formatted text from a rich text editor to an enhanced rich text column, and display it again correctly.
patch-sharepoint-rich-text-notes-from-po.fullDescription: The rich text editor control produces HTML. An enhanced rich text column in SharePoint stores HTML, so the value can be patched as is. Display uses an HTML text control, and plain-text previews need the tags removed.
patch-sharepoint-rich-text-notes-from-po.problemStatement: Notes are saved with visible tags, lose their formatting, or show as raw HTML in a gallery.
whenToUse: Notes, descriptions and comments that need bold text, lists or links
Columns set to multiple lines with enhanced rich text
Content later used in emails
whenNotToUse: Text that will be filtered or searched from the app, which works better as plain text
Columns set to plain text, where HTML shows as tags
stepByStepInstructions: Set the SharePoint column to multiple lines of text with enhanced rich text.
Add a rich text editor control and set its Default to the stored value.
Patch the editor's HtmlText to the column.
Show the value in an HTML text control, and use PlainText for previews.
Check for empty content with PlainText before saving a required note.
commonMistakes: Patching HTML into a plain text column.
Showing the column in a normal label, which displays the tags.
Checking IsBlank on HtmlText, which is not blank when it holds an empty paragraph.
troubleshooting: If tags appear in SharePoint, the column is plain text. Change it to enhanced rich text.
If formatting is lost after saving, SharePoint removed markup it does not allow, such as scripts and some styles. Keep to the editor's toolbar options.
If pasted images do not save, the editor embeds them as data that SharePoint strips. Attach images separately.
If the text is cut off, check the column is not limited and the app is not using Left on the HTML, which can break a tag.

patch-a-generated-request-number-after-c.shortDescription: Create an item, then build a readable reference such as REQ-2026-00042 from its ID and save it back.
patch-a-generated-request-number-after-c.fullDescription: SharePoint assigns the ID when the item is created, so a reference based on it needs a second write. Using the ID guarantees uniqueness, which a count of rows does not.
patch-a-generated-request-number-after-c.problemStatement: Request numbers built from CountRows or the highest existing number collide when two people submit at once.
whenToUse: Requests, tickets and orders that need a reference to quote
Numbers that must be unique without a separate counter
Apps that create items with Patch or SubmitForm
whenNotToUse: Sequences that must have no gaps or restart each year, which need a counter list updated by a flow
Lists where the plain ID is good enough
stepByStepInstructions: Add a single line of text column for the reference and index it.
Create the item and store the record that Patch returns.
Build the reference from the returned ID and Patch it back to the same item.
Show the reference to the user on a confirmation screen.
If a flow also triggers on creation, make sure it tolerates the second update.
commonMistakes: Using CountRows + 1 or Max(ID) + 1, which is neither unique nor delegable.
Reading the ID from the gallery or form instead of the record returned by Patch.
Forgetting that the second Patch triggers flows that watch for modifications.
troubleshooting: If the reference is blank, the second Patch failed or the app was closed between the two writes. A flow on item creation is a reliable backstop.
If a flow sends its email before the number exists, set the number in the flow itself, or add a trigger condition that waits for the column to be filled.
If numbers have gaps, IDs of deleted items are never reused. That is normal.
If two formats appear, more than one app or flow is writing the column. Keep the logic in one place.

patch-a-sharepoint-image-column-from-pow.shortDescription: Save a photo from the camera or Add picture control to a SharePoint Image column, and show it again in the app.
patch-a-sharepoint-image-column-from-pow.fullDescription: The SharePoint Image column type can be written from a canvas app by patching the image value directly. This pattern covers capture, save, display at different sizes and clearing the image.
patch-a-sharepoint-image-column-from-pow.problemStatement: Makers try to patch a URL or base64 text into an Image column and get a type error, or the image saves but does not display.
whenToUse: One photo per item, such as an asset, an ID photo or a product
Lists using the Image column type
Images under a few megabytes
whenNotToUse: Several photos per item. Use attachments or a document library.
Lists that still use the older Hyperlink or Picture column, which only stores a link
stepByStepInstructions: Add an Image column to the list.
Add the Add picture control or a camera to the screen.
Patch the control's image to the column.
Display the stored image using the size that fits, such as Small in galleries.
Skip the image field in the Patch when no new image was chosen.
commonMistakes: Patching a URL or text to the Image column.
Patching Blank over an existing image because the user did not pick a new one.
Using the Full size in a gallery, which is slow.
troubleshooting: If Patch reports a type mismatch, the column is the older Picture type. Create a column of type Image.
If the image does not display, reference a size property such as Photo.Medium rather than the column alone.
If large photos fail to save on mobile, reduce the camera's resolution or use the Add picture control, which compresses on some devices.
If the old image still shows after replacing it, refresh the data source. Thumbnails can take a moment to regenerate.

patch-a-sharepoint-location-text-bundle.shortDescription: Capture GPS coordinates and an address in the app and save them to plain SharePoint columns, since the Location column type is read-only.
patch-a-sharepoint-location-text-bundle.fullDescription: Canvas apps cannot write to SharePoint's Location column type. The workable pattern is a small set of ordinary columns: latitude, longitude, address text and a map link. This pattern captures the device position and saves those columns together.
patch-a-sharepoint-location-text-bundle.problemStatement: Patch to a Location column fails or is ignored, and field teams need to record where an inspection or visit took place.
whenToUse: Inspections, site visits and deliveries recorded on a phone
Records that need a map link
Lists where the Location column type is not required
whenNotToUse: Solutions that depend on the Location column's built-in address lookup
Devices without location permission
stepByStepInstructions: Add number columns for latitude and longitude, a text column for the address and a hyperlink column for the map.
Enable the location signal when the screen opens.
Capture the coordinates into variables when the user taps a button.
Patch the coordinates, address and map link together.
Show the coordinates and a button that opens the map.
commonMistakes: Trying to Patch the Location column type.
Reading Location.Latitude at save time without checking it is available.
Building the map link with a comma-decimal number format in some regions.
troubleshooting: If coordinates are blank, the user has not granted location permission, or the signal has not returned a value yet. Wait a few seconds after enabling it.
If coordinates are zero in the browser, the browser blocked location for the page.
If the map link opens the wrong place, check the order is latitude then longitude and the decimal separator is a dot. Use Text(locLat, "0.000000", "en-US").
If accuracy is poor indoors, show the coordinates and let the user correct the address text.

patch-approval-metadata-from-a-button.shortDescription: Record a decision with one button: status, approver, date and comment written in a single Patch.
patch-approval-metadata-from-a-button.fullDescription: An approve button should capture the whole decision at once, and should refuse to act if the item has already been decided. This pattern re-reads the item, checks its state and the user's right to approve, then writes all decision fields together.
patch-approval-metadata-from-a-button.problemStatement: The status changes to Approved, but nobody recorded who approved it or when, and two approvers can overwrite each other.
whenToUse: In-app approvals without a flow
Lists with approver, date and comment columns
Single-stage decisions
whenNotToUse: Approvals that must be tamper-proof, which should run in a flow under a service account
Multi-stage approvals with complex routing
stepByStepInstructions: Add approver, approved by, approved on and comment columns.
On the button, re-read the item so the check uses current data.
Stop if the item is no longer pending or the user is not the approver.
Patch the status, person, time and comment in one call.
Show the button only to the approver while the item is pending.
commonMistakes: Changing only the status and losing who decided and when.
Checking the status from a stale variable.
Relying on a hidden button as the only control over who can approve.
troubleshooting: If the person column fails to save, check the Claims value and that all six properties are present.
If two people approve at the same moment, the second save reports a conflict because the record changed. Refresh and show the current status.
If users can approve by editing the list directly, restrict list permissions and move the write into a flow.
If ApprovedOn shows the wrong time in the list, compare the site's time zone with the user's. The stored instant is the same.

patch-a-reopen-request-action.shortDescription: Let a user reopen a closed request with a reason, clearing the closure fields and counting the reopen.
patch-a-reopen-request-action.fullDescription: Reopening is more than setting the status back. This pattern checks the reopen is allowed, requires a reason, clears the closed date and resolution, increments a counter and leaves a note, so reports can tell reopened work from new work.
patch-a-reopen-request-action.problemStatement: Closed requests get reopened by editing the status, which leaves a closed date on an open item and hides how often work comes back.
whenToUse: Help desk and service request apps
Processes that measure repeat work
Requests that can be reopened within a time limit
whenNotToUse: Processes where a new linked request is the rule
Records that are archived or locked on closure
stepByStepInstructions: Add reopen count, reason and last reopened columns.
Show the button only for closed items within the reopen window and to the right people.
Ask for a reason in a dialog.
Patch the status, clear the closure fields, increment the count and log the previous resolution.
Notify the assigned person, with a flow that watches for the Reopened status.
commonMistakes: Leaving the closed date in place on a reopened item.
Losing the original resolution when clearing it.
Using Open instead of a distinct Reopened status, which hides repeat work.
troubleshooting: If Blank() does not clear the date, check formula-level error management is on in the app's settings.
If the count stays at 1, the Patch is reading a stale record. Use the current item from LookUp for the count.
If the button never shows, ClosedOn is empty on older items. Fall back to Modified.
If the assignee is not told, add a flow triggered on the status change.

patch-a-cancelled-request-status-with-re.shortDescription: Cancel a request from the app with a required reason, and record who cancelled it and when.
patch-a-cancelled-request-status-with-re.fullDescription: Cancelling should be deliberate and explained. This pattern limits who can cancel and at which stages, collects a reason from a short list plus free text, and writes the cancellation fields in one Patch.
patch-a-cancelled-request-status-with-re.problemStatement: Requests are deleted or silently set to Cancelled, so teams keep working on them and nobody knows why they were withdrawn.
whenToUse: Requests that can be withdrawn before completion
Processes that report on cancellation reasons
Apps where the requester can cancel their own items
whenNotToUse: Items that should be deleted, such as accidental drafts
Stages where cancelling needs approval
stepByStepInstructions: Add cancel reason, note, cancelled by and cancelled on columns.
Show the cancel button only at stages where cancelling is allowed and to the requester or an admin.
Collect a reason from a dropdown and a note.
Patch the status and cancellation fields together.
Use a flow to tidy up approvals and tasks that were in progress.
commonMistakes: Deleting the item instead of cancelling it.
A free-text reason only, which cannot be reported on.
Allowing cancellation after the work is complete.
troubleshooting: If the choice column fails to save, the reason text must match one of the column's choices exactly.
If the in operator shows a warning, it is evaluating a single record locally, which is fine.
If work continues after cancellation, the assignee was not told. Add the notification flow.
If a pending approval is still open, withdraw it in the follow-up flow.

patch-a-delegated-owner-field.shortDescription: Reassign a record to another person, or set a temporary delegate, by patching SharePoint person columns from a people picker.
patch-a-delegated-owner-field.fullDescription: Reassignment writes a person column, which needs the full person record. This pattern searches the directory, patches the new owner, keeps the previous owner for reference and supports a delegate with an end date.
patch-a-delegated-owner-field.problemStatement: When someone is away, their items sit untouched because reassigning means editing the list, and the person column rejects simple values.
whenToUse: Reassigning tasks, requests or approvals
Covering for absence with a delegate
Lists with a single-person owner column
whenNotToUse: Bulk reassignment of hundreds of items, which suits a flow
Ownership that comes from a group or queue
stepByStepInstructions: Add the Office 365 Users connector and a combo box that searches the directory.
Build the person record from the selected user and Patch it to the owner column.
Store the previous owner's email and the time of the change.
For cover, use a separate delegate column with an end date.
Include delegated items in the user's work view.
commonMistakes: Patching only an email address to a person column.
Losing track of who owned the item before.
Open-ended delegation with no end date.
troubleshooting: If the Patch fails for a guest, their Claims value uses a different format. Use the user principal name from the directory in the Claims string.
If the picker returns nothing, the search term is empty. isSearchTermRequired stops an expensive list of all users.
If the new owner cannot open the item, they have no permission on the list. Reassignment does not grant access.
If the delegate filter shows a delegation warning, split it into two filters and combine them in a collection.

patch-a-priority-change-with-history-not.shortDescription: Change an item's priority with a required reason, and keep a line of history showing the old and new values.
patch-a-priority-change-with-history-not.fullDescription: Priority changes affect everyone's queue, so they should be explained. This pattern only acts when the value really changed, requires a reason for escalations and prepends a dated line to a history column.
patch-a-priority-change-with-history-not.problemStatement: Priorities drift upwards with no record of who raised them or why, so the Urgent queue loses its meaning.
whenToUse: Queues ordered by priority
Teams that review escalations
Lists with a priority choice column
whenNotToUse: Priority calculated from other fields, which should not be edited directly
Apps where only a flow sets priority
stepByStepInstructions: Add a plain multi-line history column and a changed-on date.
Compare the selected priority with the stored one and stop if they match.
Require a reason when the priority is raised, and limit who can set the top level.
Patch the new priority and prepend a line with the old value, new value, person and reason.
Show the history on the detail screen.
commonMistakes: Writing a history line when nothing changed.
Requiring a reason for every change, including lowering priority, which discourages tidy-up.
Storing history in a rich text column, which complicates line handling.
troubleshooting: If the dropdown does not show the current priority, its Default must be the text value, not the choice record.
If history lines run together, display them in a multi-line label.
If the arrow character does not display in some fonts, use 'to' instead.
If priority changes made in the list are not logged, add a flow on the list for full coverage.

patch-a-due-date-extension-request.shortDescription: Let an owner ask for more time: record the requested date and reason, and apply it only when approved.
patch-a-due-date-extension-request.fullDescription: Changing a due date directly hides slippage. This pattern keeps the original date, stores the requested date and reason as a pending extension, and updates the due date only on approval, with a count of extensions.
patch-a-due-date-extension-request.problemStatement: Due dates are quietly moved, so nothing is ever late and nobody can see how often deadlines slip.
whenToUse: Tasks and actions with accountable due dates
Teams that report on-time delivery
Extensions that need a manager's agreement
whenNotToUse: Informal task lists where owners manage their own dates
Dates driven by a project schedule in another tool
stepByStepInstructions: Add columns for the original date, requested date, reason, extension status and count.
Let the owner request a later date with a reason, keeping the due date unchanged.
Save the original due date the first time an extension is requested.
On approval, copy the requested date to the due date and increment the count.
Show the extension history beside the due date and give managers a queue of requests.
commonMistakes: Letting owners edit the due date directly as well.
Overwriting the original due date on the second extension.
No limit on length or number of extensions.
troubleshooting: If the original date changes on later requests, the Coalesce is missing.
If managers do not see requests, check the manager column is filled on each item.
If owners can still change the due date in the list, make the column read-only in the form and restrict list editing.
If a reminder flow keeps chasing the old date, make sure it reads DueDate at run time.

patch-a-project-code-lookup-safely.shortDescription: Patch a SharePoint lookup column from a dropdown or typed code, checking that the target exists first.
patch-a-project-code-lookup-safely.fullDescription: A lookup column is patched with a record holding the target item's Id and Value. Saving fails, or saves blank, when the code typed by the user does not exist. This pattern validates the code, builds the lookup record and handles clearing it.
patch-a-project-code-lookup-safely.problemStatement: Users type or scan a project code, the Patch reports a type error or saves an empty lookup, and the request ends up unlinked.
whenToUse: Lookup columns to projects, cost centres, customers or assets
Codes that are typed or scanned
Reference lists too large for a simple dropdown
whenNotToUse: Small fixed sets, where a choice column is simpler
Links that do not need lookup behaviour, where a text column avoids lookup limits
stepByStepInstructions: Decide whether users pick from a list or type a code.
Find the target item with LookUp and stop with a clear message if it is missing or inactive.
Patch the lookup column with a record of Id and Value.
Set the combo box default from the stored Id when editing.
Clear the column with Blank when the link is removed.
commonMistakes: Patching the code text straight into the lookup column.
Passing only Value without the Id.
Skipping the existence check and saving a broken link.
troubleshooting: If the error says the specified column is read-only or the type is wrong, check you are patching the lookup column itself, not one of its additional fields.
If the lookup saves but shows blank, the Id does not exist in the target list.
If views fail on a large list, the list has more than 12 lookup, person and managed metadata columns in one view. Reduce them.
If the typed code never matches, compare case and stray spaces, and check the code is in the column you are searching.

patch-a-risk-score-field-from-sliders.shortDescription: Calculate a risk score from likelihood and impact sliders, show the rating live and save all three values.
patch-a-risk-score-field-from-sliders.fullDescription: A risk score is likelihood multiplied by impact, mapped to a rating band. This pattern shows the score and colour as the sliders move, and saves the inputs, the score and the rating so list views and reports can use them.
patch-a-risk-score-field-from-sliders.problemStatement: Risk registers hold a typed score that does not match the likelihood and impact beside it, and ratings are applied inconsistently.
whenToUse: Risk and issue registers
Any score built from two or three rated inputs
Lists that sort or format by rating
whenNotToUse: Scoring models with many weighted factors, which suit a calculated table or a flow
Registers where the score is calculated in SharePoint already
stepByStepInstructions: Add number columns for likelihood, impact and score, and a choice column for rating.
Add two sliders from 1 to 5 with a text label for each level.
Show the score and a coloured rating that update as the sliders move.
Save the inputs, the score and the rating together.
Require a mitigation for high scores.
commonMistakes: Saving only the score, so the inputs cannot be reviewed.
Different rating thresholds in different places. Define them once.
Leaving slider defaults empty, so editing a risk resets it to 1.
troubleshooting: If the saved rating differs from the list's own calculation, the thresholds are defined twice. Use one source.
If sliders jump back when editing, set Default from the record.
If the heat map is slow, count from a collection, not from the list.
If the rating choice fails to save, the value must match the column's choices exactly.

patch-a-calculated-display-summary-field.shortDescription: Build a one-line summary from several fields and save it to a text column for use in views, emails and search.
patch-a-calculated-display-summary-field.fullDescription: SharePoint calculated columns cannot use person, lookup or multi-line columns, and cannot be searched from Power Apps with StartsWith on combined values. Saving a summary line from the app fills that gap.
patch-a-calculated-display-summary-field.problemStatement: Views and notifications need a readable line that combines requester, category and dates, but a calculated column cannot reference the person or lookup fields.
whenToUse: List views, emails and Teams posts that need one descriptive line
Search across several fields with a single delegable StartsWith or Search
Values from person or lookup columns
whenNotToUse: Values a calculated column can already produce
Lists edited outside the app, where the summary would go stale without a flow
stepByStepInstructions: Add a single-line Summary column, and a multi-line SearchText column if you need broad search.
Build the summary text in the save formula from the form's controls.
Limit it to 255 characters for a single-line column.
Save it in the same Patch as the other fields.
Add a flow to rebuild it if the list is edited outside the app.
commonMistakes: Building the summary in several places with different formats.
Exceeding 255 characters in a single-line column.
Treating the summary as the source of truth instead of the underlying fields.
troubleshooting: If the summary is out of date, the item was edited outside the app. Add the flow.
If Search on the list shows a delegation warning, SharePoint does not delegate Search. Use StartsWith on the list, or Search on a collection.
If a part shows as blank, the control was empty. Wrap parts in Coalesce with a dash.
If dates appear in another language in the summary, pass a language tag to Text.

patch-a-requester-department-snapshot.shortDescription: Copy the requester's department, manager and job title onto the request at submit time, so reports reflect who they were then.
patch-a-requester-department-snapshot.fullDescription: Directory details change when people move teams. Saving a snapshot at submission keeps historical reports correct and avoids a directory lookup for every row in a gallery.
patch-a-requester-department-snapshot.problemStatement: Reports by department change retroactively when someone moves, and galleries that look up each requester's department are slow.
whenToUse: Reporting by department, office or cost centre
Routing based on the requester's manager
Long-lived records
whenNotToUse: Displays that should always show the person's current details
Tenants where directory fields are empty or unreliable
stepByStepInstructions: Add text columns for the snapshot fields and index the ones you filter on.
Read the user's profile and manager once at app start.
Write the snapshot fields when the request is created.
For on-behalf-of requests, read the selected person's profile instead.
Leave the snapshot alone on later edits.
commonMistakes: Looking up the department for every row in a gallery.
Refreshing the snapshot on every save, which defeats its purpose.
Not handling users with no manager, which makes ManagerV2 fail.
troubleshooting: If the department is blank, the directory has no value for that user. Store 'Unknown' and report the gap.
If ManagerV2 raises an error, the user has no manager. IfError returns blank as shown.
If guests fail the profile call, fall back to User().Email and leave the other fields empty.
If department names vary, such as 'IT' and 'Information Technology', map them through a reference list before saving.

patch-a-manager-approval-comment.shortDescription: Save a manager's decision comment to the item, required for rejections, alongside the decision fields.
patch-a-manager-approval-comment.fullDescription: A decision without a comment leaves the requester guessing. This pattern checks the user is the item's manager, requires a meaningful comment for rejections and returns, and saves the comment with the decision in one Patch.
patch-a-manager-approval-comment.problemStatement: Rejected requests come back with no explanation, so requesters resubmit the same thing or chase the manager by email.
whenToUse: Manager approvals handled inside the app
Decisions the requester needs to understand
Lists with a manager person column per item
whenNotToUse: Approvals that run in the Approvals connector, which collects comments itself
Confidential comments the requester must not see, which need a separate restricted list
stepByStepInstructions: Add a manager comment column and a decision date.
Let the manager choose approve, reject or return, and adjust the comment prompt to match.
Check the user is the manager and the item is still awaiting a decision.
Require a comment for anything other than approval, then Patch the decision and comment together.
Show the decision and comment to the requester.
commonMistakes: Making comments optional for rejections.
Saving the comment in a separate step that can fail after the status has changed.
Showing an error under the comment box before the user has tried to save.
troubleshooting: If the manager check fails for the right person, compare the emails in a label. Aliases and guest addresses can differ.
If the comment is cut off, the column is single line.
If the requester is not notified, add a flow on the status change that includes the comment.

If line breaks in the comment are lost in emails, replace Char(10) with
in the flow.

patch-a-conditional-required-field-set.shortDescription: Require different fields depending on a category or status, and only save the fields that apply.
patch-a-conditional-required-field-set.fullDescription: Many forms need extra fields only in some cases, such as a cost centre for purchases or a justification above a threshold. This pattern defines the rules in one table, shows and requires the right inputs, and clears values that no longer apply.
patch-a-conditional-required-field-set.problemStatement: The list cannot mark fields as required only some of the time, so the form either asks for everything or lets incomplete records through.
whenToUse: Forms that branch by request type, status or amount
Rules that would be awkward as SharePoint validation
Custom forms saved with Patch
whenNotToUse: Fields that are always required, which the list can enforce
Rules that must hold for edits outside the app
stepByStepInstructions: List which fields each type or condition needs in one rules table.
Show each conditional input only when its rule applies.
On save, collect the required fields that are empty for the current type.
Stop with a message naming the missing fields, or Patch.
Clear fields that do not apply to the chosen type so old values are not left behind.
commonMistakes: Hiding a field but still saving the value typed before the type was changed.
Repeating the same condition in Visible, Required and the save formula with small differences.
Marking the columns as required in SharePoint, which then blocks types that do not use them.
troubleshooting: If a hidden field still blocks saving, it is marked required in the list. Remove that and enforce it in the app.
If old values remain after changing type, add the If with Blank for each conditional field.
If the missing list is empty but a field is blank, its rule row is missing or the type text does not match.
If the amount comparison errors on empty input, wrap it as Value(Coalesce(txtAmount.Text, "0")).

patch-a-related-document-link-field.shortDescription: Save a link to a document in a SharePoint hyperlink column, with validation and a button to open it.
patch-a-related-document-link-field.fullDescription: A hyperlink column is patched with the URL as text. The display text cannot be set from a canvas app, so this pattern stores a separate title column where a friendly name is needed, validates the link and opens it with Launch.
patch-a-related-document-link-field.problemStatement: Links are pasted into a notes field, cannot be clicked from the app, and are often incomplete or point at a local file path.
whenToUse: Linking a request to a contract, specification or folder
Documents that live in a library or another system
One or two links per item
whenNotToUse: Many links per item, which belong in a child list
Files that should be uploaded with the item as attachments
stepByStepInstructions: Add a hyperlink column and a text column for the link's title.
Validate that the text is an https address within the length limit.
Patch the URL as text to the hyperlink column and the title to its own column.
Add a button that opens the link in a new tab with Launch.
Optionally let users pick a file from a library and take its link.
commonMistakes: Passing a record with Url and Description, which the hyperlink column does not accept from Power Apps.
Accepting local paths such as C: drives.
Saving very long sharing links that exceed the column's 255 characters.
troubleshooting: If the list shows the URL as its own display text, that is expected from Power Apps. Use the title column in views, or set the description with a flow.
If Launch does nothing, the value is missing https:// at the start.
If the link is rejected as too long, use the document's direct path or a short sharing link.
If users cannot open the document, the link is valid but they lack permission on the file.

patch-a-training-completion-acknowledgem.shortDescription: Record that a user has read and acknowledged a policy or completed training, once per person and version.
patch-a-training-completion-acknowledgem.fullDescription: An acknowledgement is a row that says who agreed to which version and when. This pattern checks for an existing row, requires the tick box and writes the acknowledgement with details that make it useful as evidence.
patch-a-training-completion-acknowledgem.problemStatement: Acknowledgements collected by email or a show of hands cannot be reported on, and people acknowledge the same policy twice or not at all.
whenToUse: Policy sign-off and mandatory reading
Short training modules with a confirmation
Evidence needed for audit
whenNotToUse: Formal learning records held in a learning management system
Legally binding signatures, which need a signature service
stepByStepInstructions: Create a policies list with a version, and an acknowledgements list keyed by policy, version and user.
Check whether the user has already acknowledged the current version.
Require the user to open the document and tick the statement before confirming.
Write one acknowledgement row with the exact statement, version and time.
Show the user their status and list what is still outstanding.
commonMistakes: Storing acknowledgement as a yes/no column on the policy, which cannot hold one answer per person.
Ignoring versions, so an old acknowledgement appears to cover a new policy.
Allowing users to edit or delete their acknowledgement rows.
troubleshooting: If duplicates appear, the check ran against stale data. Repeat the LookUp immediately before the Patch as shown, and set unique values on a combined key column if needed.
If users can alter records, set the list's item-level permissions so users can create items but not edit them.
If the outstanding list shows a delegation warning, load the user's acknowledgements into a collection first.
If the time shows differently in the list, it is the same instant in the site's time zone.

patch-a-service-catalog-selection.shortDescription: Let users choose a service from a catalogue and copy its details, such as fulfilment team and target days, onto the request.
patch-a-service-catalog-selection.fullDescription: A service catalogue list drives the request form: categories filter services, the chosen service supplies defaults and routing, and those values are saved on the request so later catalogue changes do not rewrite history.
patch-a-service-catalog-selection.problemStatement: Requests arrive as free text, so they cannot be routed automatically and every one needs triage.
whenToUse: IT, HR and facilities request apps
Routing and targets that depend on the service chosen
Catalogues maintained by the business
whenNotToUse: A handful of fixed request types, where a choice column is enough
Catalogues held in a service management tool with its own portal
patch-a-service-catalog-selection.formulaOrCode:
List: Service Catalog
  Title | Category (Choice) | Description | FulfilmentTeam (Text) | TeamEmail | TargetDays (Number)
  NeedsApproval (Yes/No) | IsActive (Yes/No) | SortOrder

// Load once
ClearCollect(colCatalog, Filter('Service Catalog', IsActive = true));

// Category tiles or dropdown
ddCategory.Items : Sort(Distinct(colCatalog, Category.Value), Value)

// Services for the category, with search
galServices.Items :
    SortByColumns(
        Filter(colCatalog,
            Category.Value = ddCategory.Selected.Value,
            IsBlank(txtFind.Text) || txtFind.Text in Title || txtFind.Text in Description),
        "SortOrder")
galServices.OnSelect : UpdateContext({ locService: ThisItem })

// Show what the user can expect
lblExpect.Text :
    locService.Description & Char(10) &
    "Handled by " & locService.FulfilmentTeam & ". Usually completed within " & locService.TargetDays & " working days." &
    If(locService.NeedsApproval, " Needs your manager's approval first.")

// Submit: copy the catalogue values onto the request
If(
    IsBlank(locService),
    Notify("Choose a service", NotificationType.Error),
    IfError(
        Set(varRecord,
            Patch(Requests, Defaults(Requests), {
                Title:          locService.Title & " - " & User().FullName,
                Service:        { Id: locService.ID, Value: locService.Title },      // lookup column
                ServiceName:    locService.Title,                                     // snapshot text
                Category:       locService.Category,
                FulfilmentTeam: locService.FulfilmentTeam,
                TeamEmail:      locService.TeamEmail,
                TargetDate:     DateAdd(Today(), locService.TargetDays, TimeUnit.Days),
                Status:         { Value: If(locService.NeedsApproval, "Awaiting approval", "Submitted") },
                Details:        txtDetails.Text
            })
        );
        Navigate(scrConfirmation),
        Notify("Could not submit: " & FirstError.Message, NotificationType.Error)
    )
)
stepByStepInstructions: Create the catalogue list with routing and target fields for each service.
Load active services into a collection.
Let users pick a category, then a service, and show what to expect.
On submit, copy the service's team, target and approval need onto the request.
Route on the copied fields in your flow.
commonMistakes: Saving only a lookup to the service, so changing the catalogue changes old requests.
Listing every service in one long dropdown.
Leaving retired services selectable.
troubleshooting: If the lookup fails to save, pass both Id and Value. If the lookup is not needed, keep only the text snapshot.
If the search shows a delegation warning, it is running on the collection, which is fine.
If the target date lands on a weekend, calculate working days in the flow or with a working-day formula.
If a new service does not appear, the collection was loaded before it was added. Reload the catalogue.

patch-a-pmo-triage-assignment.shortDescription: Triage an incoming request in one action: set the category, priority, assignee and due date, and move it out of the new queue.
patch-a-pmo-triage-assignment.fullDescription: Triage is the step where a new request gets an owner. This pattern gives the triage lead a single panel, suggests an assignee from the category, and writes all triage fields in one Patch with a guard against two people triaging the same item.
patch-a-pmo-triage-assignment.problemStatement: New requests wait in a shared inbox, two people pick up the same one, and others are never assigned.
whenToUse: Intake queues for a PMO, service desk or shared team
A triage role that assigns work to others
Requests that need categorising before work starts
whenNotToUse: Queues where people assign themselves
Routing that is fully rule-based, which a flow can do without a person
stepByStepInstructions: Show new requests oldest first with how long each has waited.
Add category, priority, assignee and due date inputs with sensible suggestions.
On assign, re-read the item and stop if someone else has triaged it.
Patch all triage fields and the new status together.
Notify the assignee with a flow on the status change.
commonMistakes: Assigning without changing the status, so the item stays in the new queue.
No check for a second triager.
Leaving the due date empty.
troubleshooting: If two people triage the same item, the re-read check stops the second. Refresh the queue afterwards.
If the suggested assignee is blank, the routing list has no row for that category.
If the queue is slow, limit it to the status filter, which is delegable, and index the status column.
If the workload count is wrong, the open-items collection is stale. Reload it when the screen opens.

build-a-queue-dashboard-gallery.shortDescription: Build a work queue screen with count tiles, an oldest-first gallery and age highlighting.
build-a-queue-dashboard-gallery.fullDescription: A queue dashboard shows a team what needs attention now. This pattern loads the open items once, shows counts per status as tiles that also act as filters, and highlights items by how long they have waited.
build-a-queue-dashboard-gallery.problemStatement: The team works from a SharePoint view with no sense of what is urgent, how much is waiting or what has been untouched for days.
whenToUse: Shared team queues
Processes with service targets
Open item counts below the data row limit
whenNotToUse: Queues with many thousands of open items, which need server-side counts from a flow or Power BI
Personal task lists
build-a-queue-dashboard-gallery.formulaOrCode:
// Screen.OnVisible: load open work once (status filter is delegable)
ClearCollect(
    colQueue,
    AddColumns(
        Filter(Requests, Status.Value <> "Closed" && Status.Value <> "Cancelled"),
        AgeDays, DateDiff(Created, Now(), TimeUnit.Days),
        StatusText, Status.Value,
        OwnerName, Coalesce(AssignedTo.DisplayName, "Unassigned")
    )
);
UpdateContext({ locStatus: "All" })

// Tiles (horizontal gallery)
Items :
    Table(
        { Label: "All",         Count: CountRows(colQueue) },
        { Label: "New",         Count: CountRows(Filter(colQueue, StatusText = "New")) },
        { Label: "In progress", Count: CountRows(Filter(colQueue, StatusText = "In progress")) },
        { Label: "Waiting",     Count: CountRows(Filter(colQueue, StatusText = "Waiting")) },
        { Label: "Unassigned",  Count: CountRows(Filter(colQueue, OwnerName = "Unassigned")) },
        { Label: "Over 5 days", Count: CountRows(Filter(colQueue, AgeDays > 5)) }
    )
OnSelect     : UpdateContext({ locStatus: ThisItem.Label })
TemplateFill : If(ThisItem.Label = locStatus, RGBA(15, 108, 189, 0.12), Color.White)

// Queue gallery
Items :
    SortByColumns(
        Filter(
            colQueue,
            locStatus = "All"
                || StatusText = locStatus
                || (locStatus = "Unassigned" && OwnerName = "Unassigned")
                || (locStatus = "Over 5 days" && AgeDays > 5),
            IsBlank(txtSearch.Text) || txtSearch.Text in Title
        ),
        "AgeDays", SortOrder.Descending
    )

// Row
lblAge.Text  : If(ThisItem.AgeDays = 0, "Today", ThisItem.AgeDays & " d")
lblAge.Color : If(ThisItem.AgeDays > 5, RGBA(196, 49, 75, 1), ThisItem.AgeDays > 2, RGBA(188, 100, 0, 1), RGBA(96, 94, 92, 1))
lblOwner.Text: ThisItem.OwnerName

// Refresh
icoRefresh.OnSelect : Refresh(Requests); Select(btnLoadQueue)      // btnLoadQueue holds the ClearCollect

// Warn if the queue may be cut off
lblLimit.Visible : CountRows(colQueue) >= 2000
stepByStepInstructions: Load open items into a collection with age, status text and owner name added.
Build tiles from a table of labels and counts, and store the selected label.
Filter the gallery by the selected tile and search text, oldest first.
Colour the age by threshold.
Add a refresh icon and a warning when the collection reaches the row limit.
commonMistakes: Counting rows directly on the SharePoint list, which is not delegable.
Loading closed items as well, which wastes the row limit.
