Sorting newest first, so old items sink out of sight.
troubleshooting: If counts look low, the open set exceeds the data row limit. Raise it to 2,000 in Settings or narrow the filter.
If the status filter shows a delegation warning, use separate not-equals conditions as shown rather than the in operator.
If the queue looks stale, reload on OnVisible and after each update.
If the gallery is slow, remove controls from the row template and keep the collection to the columns needed with ShowColumns.

build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.shortDescription: Split a long record across tabs such as Details, Activity and Files on one screen.
build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.fullDescription: Tabs keep a detailed record readable without several screens. One variable holds the selected tab, a horizontal gallery draws the tab bar, and each tab's content sits in a container that shows only when selected.
build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.problemStatement: A detail screen has become a long scroll of fields, comments and attachments, and users cannot find what they need.
whenToUse: Records with distinct groups of information
Screens that combine fields, history and files
Tablet and desktop layouts
whenNotToUse: Short records that fit on one view
Steps that must be completed in order, which suit a wizard
stepByStepInstructions: Create a context variable for the selected tab.
Add a horizontal gallery of tab labels that sets the variable.
Put each tab's controls in its own container and set Visible from the variable.
Load heavier data when its tab is first opened.
Keep shared buttons such as Save outside the tab containers.
commonMistakes: Separate screens per tab, which lose unsaved input when switching.
Loading every tab's data up front.
Validation errors on a hidden tab that the user cannot see.
troubleshooting: If inputs lose their values when switching tabs, they are being reset by a changing Default. Hiding a container does not clear its controls.
If a hidden tab's required field blocks saving, flag the tab with an error marker and switch to it.
If the tab bar overflows on phones, make the gallery scroll horizontally or use a dropdown below a width breakpoint.
If the tab is blank on open, pass locTab in Navigate or set the default in OnVisible.

build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.shortDescription: Design a request form that works on a phone: one column, large touch targets, the right keyboard and a fixed submit bar.
build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.fullDescription: Phone forms fail when they are shrunken desktop forms. This pattern uses a vertical auto-layout container, full-width inputs sized for touch, input types that bring up the right keyboard and a submit bar that stays in view.
build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.problemStatement: Field staff struggle with tiny controls, a keyboard that hides the input and a Submit button somewhere below the fold.
whenToUse: Apps used mainly on phones
Short capture forms completed on the move
Forms that include photos or location
whenNotToUse: Long data entry best done at a desk
Forms needing wide tables or side-by-side comparison
stepByStepInstructions: Lay the screen out as header, scrolling body and fixed footer.
Stack fields in one column with inputs at least 44 to 48 high and stretched to full width.
Set keyboard modes so number and email fields open the right keyboard.
Replace short dropdowns with tap buttons and pre-fill what you can.
Keep Submit in the footer, disabled until the minimum is entered, and clear the form after sending.
commonMistakes: Two columns of fields on a phone.
Small icons as the only way to act.
A submit button inside the scrolling area.
troubleshooting: If the keyboard covers the input, make sure the input sits inside a scrollable container so the player can move it into view.
If the numeric keyboard does not appear, set both Format and VirtualKeyboardMode on classic text inputs.
If the layout breaks in landscape, lock orientation in Settings or use auto-layout containers.
If photos are slow to upload, lower the camera resolution or use the Add picture control.

build-a-reusable-filter-panel.shortDescription: Add a slide-in filter panel with status, owner and date filters that apply together and can be cleared in one tap.
build-a-reusable-filter-panel.fullDescription: A filter panel keeps the main screen clean while offering several filters. This pattern holds the applied filters in one record variable, applies them in a single delegable Filter, and shows how many are active.
build-a-reusable-filter-panel.problemStatement: Filters are scattered across the top of the screen, each change reloads the gallery, and users cannot tell which filters are on.
whenToUse: Galleries with three or more filters
Phone layouts with little room
Filters that should apply together with an Apply button
whenNotToUse: One or two filters, which are fine inline
Data that cannot be filtered delegably and is too large to collect
stepByStepInstructions: Hold the applied filters in one record variable with defaults.
Build a panel container with the filter controls, Apply and Clear.
Copy control values into the record on Apply and close the panel.
Write the gallery's Filter so each condition is skipped when its filter is at the default.
Show a badge with the number of active filters.
commonMistakes: Binding the gallery directly to the panel's controls, so it reloads on every change.
Filter logic that is not delegable, such as the in operator on a column.
No indication that filters are active.
troubleshooting: If a delegation warning appears, test each condition on its own to find the one that is not delegable.
If the date filter misses the last day, compare with the day after the end date as shown.
If Clear does not reset a control, its Default must read from the filter record.
If filtering unassigned items misses rows, test the person column with AssignedTo.Email = Blank() or keep a text copy of the owner's email.

build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.shortDescription: Break a long form into steps on one screen, validate each step and review everything before submitting.
build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.fullDescription: A wizard keeps a long intake manageable. All steps live on one screen so input is never lost, a variable tracks the current step, each Next validates its step, and the last step shows a summary before one Patch.
build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.problemStatement: A single long form is abandoned halfway, and a form split across screens loses data when users go back.
whenToUse: Intake forms with more than eight to ten fields
Forms where later questions depend on earlier answers
Processes that benefit from a review step
whenNotToUse: Short forms
Expert users who prefer everything on one page
stepByStepInstructions: Group the fields into three to five steps and define them in a table.
Place each step in its own container on one screen, shown by a step variable.
Add a progress indicator and a heading showing the step number.
Validate the current step before moving on.
Finish with a read-only review and a single Patch on submit.
commonMistakes: One screen per step, which loses input and repeats layout.
Validating only at the end, sending users back to hunt for errors.
No way to go back and change an earlier answer.
troubleshooting: If values vanish when moving between steps, a control's Default is tied to something that changes. Hidden containers keep their values.
If a skipped step still blocks submission, exclude its fields from the final checks.
If users lose work when the app closes, save a draft at each Next with Patch and a Draft status.
If the progress gallery shows numbers as decimals, wrap the number in Text().

build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.shortDescription: Let users add several line items to a collection, review and edit them, then save them all at once.
build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.fullDescription: Line items such as order lines or expense rows are easier to enter when nothing is saved until the user is ready. This pattern keeps the rows in a collection, supports add, edit and remove, shows a running total and writes everything with a bulk Patch.
build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.problemStatement: Each line is written to SharePoint as it is added, so abandoned entries leave orphan rows and every change waits on a network call.
whenToUse: Header and line item entry, such as orders, expenses and timesheets
Batches the user wants to check before committing
Up to a few hundred rows
whenNotToUse: Rows that other users must see immediately
Sessions long enough that losing unsaved rows would be costly, unless you add a draft save
stepByStepInstructions: Collect each new line into a collection with its own key.
Show the collection in a gallery with inline edit and remove.
Display a running count and total.
On save, create the header, then write all lines with one Patch.
Clear the collection only after a successful save.
commonMistakes: Writing each line to the list as it is added.
Clearing the collection before confirming the save worked.
Calling Patch once per row inside ForAll.
troubleshooting: If the bulk Patch fails with a type error, the record shape does not match the list's columns. Check names and types.
If only some lines are saved, compare the count in the list with the collection and offer a retry for the rest.
If inline edits do not stick, the row is being patched by a stale reference. Use ThisItem inside the gallery.
If users lose lines when the app closes, save the collection with SaveData on change and reload it with LoadData.

build-an-approval-history-timeline.shortDescription: Show a request's approval steps as a vertical timeline with who decided, when and what they said.
build-an-approval-history-timeline.fullDescription: A timeline answers where a request is and how it got there. This pattern reads decision rows from a history list, sorts them, and draws each as a dot, a connecting line and a card, with pending steps shown differently.
build-an-approval-history-timeline.problemStatement: Requesters cannot see which approval stage their request has reached or who it is waiting on.
whenToUse: Multi-stage approvals
Processes where requesters ask for status
History stored one row per decision
whenNotToUse: Single-step approvals, where one line of text is enough
Histories kept only as text in a notes column
build-an-approval-history-timeline.formulaOrCode:
List: Approval History
  Title | RequestId (Number, indexed) | Stage (Text) | StageOrder (Number) | Outcome (Choice: Pending, Approved, Rejected, Returned)
  ApproverName | ApproverEmail | DecidedOn (Date and time) | Comments

// Load for the open request
ClearCollect(
    colTimeline,
    SortByColumns(Filter('Approval History', RequestId = varRecord.ID), "StageOrder", SortOrder.Ascending)
)

// Vertical gallery: galTimeline.Items = colTimeline, flexible height, TemplatePadding 0

// Dot (circle)
Fill : Switch(ThisItem.Outcome.Value,
         "Approved", RGBA(16, 124, 16, 1),
         "Rejected", RGBA(196, 49, 75, 1),
         "Returned", RGBA(255, 185, 0, 1),
         RGBA(200, 198, 196, 1))                       // Pending

// Icon inside the dot
Icon : Switch(ThisItem.Outcome.Value, "Approved", Icon.Check, "Rejected", Icon.Cancel, "Returned", Icon.Reload, Icon.Clock)

// Connector line (thin rectangle below the dot)
Visible : ThisItem.StageOrder <> Last(colTimeline).StageOrder
Height  : Parent.TemplateHeight

// Card text
lblStage.Text  : ThisItem.Stage
lblWho.Text    : If(ThisItem.Outcome.Value = "Pending",
                    "Waiting for " & ThisItem.ApproverName,
                    ThisItem.Outcome.Value & " by " & ThisItem.ApproverName)
lblWhen.Text   : If(IsBlank(ThisItem.DecidedOn), "",
                    Text(ThisItem.DecidedOn, "d mmm yyyy, hh:mm") &
                    " (" & DateDiff(ThisItem.DecidedOn, Now(), TimeUnit.Days) & " days ago)")
lblComment.Text    : ThisItem.Comments
lblComment.Visible : !IsBlank(ThisItem.Comments)

// Summary above the timeline
lblSummary.Text :
    With({ pending: First(Filter(colTimeline, Outcome.Value = "Pending")) },
         If(IsBlank(pending), "All approval steps are complete.",
            "Currently with " & pending.ApproverName & " (" & pending.Stage & ")"))

// How long each stage took
DateDiff(LookUp(colTimeline, StageOrder = ThisItem.StageOrder - 1).DecidedOn, ThisItem.DecidedOn, TimeUnit.Hours) & " h"
stepByStepInstructions: Store each approval decision as a row in a history list, including pending steps.
Load the rows for the request, sorted by stage order.
Draw each row with a coloured dot, a connector line and a text card in a flexible-height gallery.
Show pending stages in grey with who they are waiting for.
Add a one-line summary of the current stage above the timeline.
commonMistakes: Showing only completed steps, so users cannot see what is still to come.
Fixed-height rows that cut off long comments.
Reading history from the list for every row instead of a collection.
troubleshooting: If the connector line has gaps, set the gallery's template padding to 0 and the line height to the template height.
If rows are in the wrong order, sort by a numeric stage order, not by title.
If comments are cut off, use a flexible-height gallery and auto-height labels.
If the filter shows a delegation warning, RequestId must be a number column compared with a number.

build-a-requester-self-service-screen.shortDescription: Give requesters one screen to track their requests and act on them: add information, withdraw or confirm completion.
build-a-requester-self-service-screen.fullDescription: Self-service reduces status emails. This pattern shows the requester's items with the next action expected of them, and offers only the actions that are valid for each status, each saved with a note.
build-a-requester-self-service-screen.problemStatement: Requesters email the team to ask for updates, add details or cancel, and the team re-keys those changes.
whenToUse: Request and ticket apps with a requester role
Processes where requesters must respond to queries
Teams that want fewer status emails
whenNotToUse: Processes where requesters must not change a submitted request
Apps used only by the fulfilment team
stepByStepInstructions: Load the user's own requests and flag the ones waiting on them.
Sort those to the top and say what is needed.
Offer add information, withdraw, confirm and reopen only in the statuses where each is valid.
Save each action as a status change with a note.
Describe the current status in plain language with the person it is waiting on.
commonMistakes: Letting requesters edit any field at any stage.
Showing internal status names that mean nothing to requesters.
Actions that change the status without telling the team.
troubleshooting: If requesters can act on other people's items, the filter is the only guard. Add list permissions or item-level permissions for real protection.
If the team is not told about new information, add a flow on the status change back to Submitted.
If the in operator against a list of statuses raises a warning, it is evaluated on the collection or a single record, which is fine.
If a requester cannot save, they need edit permission on their own items.

build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.shortDescription: Give administrators a safe place to find and fix bad records in bulk, with a preview and a log of what changed.
build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.fullDescription: Data problems recur: missing owners, invalid statuses, orphaned child rows. This pattern defines each known problem as a check with a query and a fix, shows the affected records first, applies the fix in bulk and logs it.
build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.problemStatement: Fixing bad data means editing rows one at a time in the list, with no record of what was changed.
whenToUse: Apps with recurring data quality problems
After a migration or schema change
Admins who are not comfortable with scripts
whenNotToUse: One-off fixes, which are quicker in grid view
Changes to thousands of rows, which suit a flow or script
stepByStepInstructions: List the known data problems and write a query for each.
Show the matching records for review before anything changes.
Enable the fix only after a preview of the same check.
Apply the fix as one bulk Patch using each record's ID.
Write the check name, count and record IDs to an admin log.
commonMistakes: Fixing without a preview.
No log, so nobody knows what was changed or when.
Running against more rows than the delegation limit returns and assuming everything is fixed.
troubleshooting: If the count stops at 500 or 2,000, more records remain. Run the check again until it returns none.
If the bulk Patch changes nothing, include the ID in each record so Patch knows which row to update.
If a filter on a blank person or date shows a warning, the list is being filtered locally. Narrow it with a delegable status filter first.
If a fix triggers many flow runs, add trigger conditions to those flows or pause them while repairing.

build-a-printable-request-summary.shortDescription: Create a clean, print-ready view of a record and save it as a PDF or send it to the printer.
build-a-printable-request-summary.fullDescription: Canvas apps can print a screen with Print(), or turn a screen or container into a PDF with the PDF function. This pattern builds a dedicated print layout, hides on-screen controls and offers both print and save to SharePoint.
build-a-printable-request-summary.problemStatement: Users take screenshots of the app to share or file a request, and the result includes buttons and cut-off text.
whenToUse: Records that must be filed, signed or shared outside the app
Summaries for meetings
Single-record output
whenNotToUse: Pixel-perfect or multi-record documents, which suit a Word template populated by a flow
Long tables that span many pages
stepByStepInstructions: Create a separate screen laid out like a page, with a white background and no navigation.
Bind labels and HTML text controls to the record, using auto height for long text.
Add a Print button that calls Print and hides itself using the screen's Printing property.
For a file, generate a PDF of the screen and pass it to a flow that saves it to a library.
Test with long content and with different page sizes.
commonMistakes: Printing the normal working screen with its buttons and scroll bars.
Using galleries for long tables, which cut off at the visible area.
Expecting Print to control paper size. The browser's print dialog does that.
troubleshooting: If content is cut off, use auto-height controls and set ExpandContainers to true in the PDF call.
If the PDF function is not recognised, enable it under Settings, in the upcoming features list for your app version.
If images are missing from the PDF, they are loaded from a source that needs sign-in. Use images stored in the app or in a column.
If Print does nothing on mobile, printing is supported in web browsers. Offer the PDF route on phones.

use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.shortDescription: Show progress while a flow runs from a button, block repeat taps, and handle the result or failure.
use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.fullDescription: Calling a flow from an app is synchronous: the formula waits for the response. This pattern sets a busy state around the call, captures the flow's response, handles errors and timeouts, and re-enables the screen.
use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.problemStatement: Users tap the button again because nothing seems to happen, the flow runs twice, and failures pass unnoticed.
whenToUse: Buttons that call a flow and wait for a result
Flows that take a few seconds
Actions that must not run twice
whenNotToUse: Long-running work over two minutes, which should be started and tracked through a status column instead
Fire-and-forget flows where the app does not need the result
stepByStepInstructions: Set a busy variable before calling the flow and clear it afterwards.
Store the flow's response in a variable.
Have the flow always respond, with a success flag and a message.
Wrap the call in IfError to catch connection failures and timeouts.
Disable the button while busy and once the record has moved on.
commonMistakes: A flow with no Respond action, so the app cannot tell what happened.
Leaving the busy state on when the call fails.
Waiting on a flow that takes minutes, which times out.
troubleshooting: If the call times out after about two minutes, the flow is too slow to wait for. Respond early and poll a status column.
If response fields are not recognised, remove and re-add the flow in the app after changing its Respond action.
If the flow ran but the app shows an error, a later action failed after the response was sent. Send the response last, or check the run history.
If the flow runs twice, the button was tapped twice before the busy state applied. Also guard in the flow with a status check.

use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.shortDescription: Navigate only after a save has succeeded, using the record Patch returns or the form's OnSuccess.
use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.fullDescription: Chaining Navigate straight after Patch moves the user on even when the save failed. This pattern captures the result, checks it, and then navigates with the saved record, including its new ID.
use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.problemStatement: The app shows the confirmation screen although the record was never saved, or opens the detail screen with a blank record.
whenToUse: Any save followed by navigation
Screens that need the new item's ID
Custom forms and edit forms alike
whenNotToUse: Saves that keep the user on the same screen
Background saves where the result is not needed immediately
stepByStepInstructions: Store the result of Patch in a variable.
Wrap the save in IfError, or check Errors for the data source.
Navigate only in the success branch, passing the saved record.
With an edit form, navigate from OnSuccess, not from the button.
Use the saved record's values to choose where to go.
commonMistakes: Writing Patch(...); Navigate(...) so navigation happens regardless.
Calling SubmitForm and Navigate in the same button.
Reading the new ID from the gallery or by taking the last row of the list.
troubleshooting: If the next screen shows a blank record, the variable was set from the form's controls instead of the Patch result.
If navigation happens despite an error, the Navigate sits outside the IfError.
If OnSuccess never fires, validation failed. Show the form's Error in OnFailure.
If Last(DataSource) returns someone else's record, stop using it. The Patch result is the only reliable source of the new ID.

use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.shortDescription: Turn features on or off, for everyone or for a pilot group, from a SharePoint list without republishing.
use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.fullDescription: Feature flags let you ship a feature hidden, enable it for testers, then for everyone. This pattern stores flags in a list with an optional pilot audience, loads them once and exposes each as a boolean named formula.
use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.problemStatement: A half-finished feature blocks a release, or a new feature has to go to everyone at once with no way to switch it off.
whenToUse: Gradual rollouts and pilots
Features that may need to be turned off quickly
Different behaviour per environment
whenNotToUse: Security controls. A hidden button does not protect data.
Permanent configuration, where a settings list entry is clearer than a flag
stepByStepInstructions: Create a Feature Flags list with a name, an enabled switch and an optional pilot list.
Load it into a collection at start.
Expose each flag as a named formula that is true when enabled or when the user is in the pilot.
Use the formula in Visible, DisplayMode and If conditions.
Remove the flag and the old code path once a feature is fully released.
commonMistakes: Leaving flags in place for years until nobody knows what they do.
Defaulting a missing flag to on.
Using a flag to hide a feature that users must not access, without securing the data.
troubleshooting: If a flag change does not take effect, the app loads flags at start. Restart the app.
If a pilot user does not see the feature, check for spaces or a different email alias in the pilot list.
If the collection is empty on first use in a named formula, reference the list directly in the formula instead.
If testers and everyone else must differ per environment, keep a separate flags list in each environment's site.

use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.shortDescription: Hold files in a collection while the user fills in a new request, then upload them once the item exists.
use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.fullDescription: Attachments belong to an item, and a new item has no ID until it is saved. This pattern gathers files in a collection, shows them with remove buttons and size checks, and uploads them after the item is created, with the form control or a flow.
use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.problemStatement: Users cannot attach files to a custom form for a new item, or the files vanish when the form is saved with Patch.
whenToUse: Custom forms that save with Patch
Photos captured in the app
Files that should go to a document library
whenNotToUse: Standard edit forms, where the attachments card and SubmitForm already work
Very large files that will not fit in device memory
stepByStepInstructions: Decide between reusing the form's attachment card with Patch, or your own collection with a flow.
Collect each chosen file or photo with a name and its content.
Show the files with a remove option and enforce count and size limits.
Create the item first and keep the returned record.
Upload each file against the new ID, then clear the collection.
commonMistakes: Expecting Patch to accept a table of files for the Attachments column without the form's Updates.
Uploading before the item exists.
Clearing the collection before the uploads finish.
troubleshooting: If the flow receives an empty file, pass the content from the attachment control's Value or the camera's Photo, inside a file record as shown.
If uploads are slow, each file is a separate flow run. Keep files small, or send all files to one flow run as an array.
If files over a certain size fail, check the list attachment limit of 250 MB and the practical memory limits of the device.
If the notification reports zero files, the collection was cleared first. Show the message before Clear, as in the sample.

use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.shortDescription: Show, hide and disable approve and reject buttons based on status and role, and say why an action is unavailable.
use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.fullDescription: Approval buttons should reflect what the current user can do right now. This pattern works out the allowed actions once from the item's status and the user's role, drives every button from that, and explains disabled states.
use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.problemStatement: Users see approve buttons on items they cannot approve, tap them and get an error, or see no buttons and do not know why.
whenToUse: Screens with approve, reject, return or withdraw actions
Several roles viewing the same record
Statuses that limit what can happen next
whenNotToUse: Screens with a single always-available action
As a replacement for server-side permission checks
stepByStepInstructions: List each action and the status and role that allow it.
Calculate a record of allowed actions when the screen opens and after each save.
Set each button's Visible and DisplayMode from that record.
Show a short sentence explaining why no action is available.
Re-check the item's current status when the button is pressed.
commonMistakes: Repeating slightly different conditions on each button.
Hiding everything with no explanation.
Trusting the button state alone, with no check at save time.
troubleshooting: If buttons do not update after a save, recalculate the allowed actions once the record variable changes.
If an approver sees disabled buttons, compare the approver email on the item with their sign-in.
If two people act at once, the re-check stops the second and refreshes their view.
If someone approves by editing the list directly, button states are not security. Lock down the list or move the write to a flow.

use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.shortDescription: Show a clear fallback such as Unassigned, and a default avatar, when a person column is empty.
use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.fullDescription: An empty person column is a blank record, so labels show nothing and photo lookups raise errors. This pattern uses Coalesce and IsBlank to show fallback text, initials or a generic icon, and handles multi-person columns.
use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.problemStatement: Galleries show empty gaps where an owner should be, and photo controls throw errors for rows with no person.
whenToUse: Galleries and detail screens showing assignees, approvers or managers
Optional person columns
User photos from Office 365 Users
whenNotToUse: Required person columns that are never empty
Screens where an empty value should stay visually empty
stepByStepInstructions: Wrap person display names in Coalesce with a fallback.
Style the fallback differently so missing owners stand out.
Guard photo lookups with a blank check and IfError.
Use IsEmpty for multi-person columns.
Hide contact actions when there is nobody to contact.
commonMistakes: Calling UserPhotoV2 with a blank email.
Testing a multi-person column with IsBlank instead of IsEmpty.
Showing the same fallback whether the item is new or long overdue for an owner.
troubleshooting: If the photo control shows an error icon, the user has no photo or the email is a guest's. IfError supplies the fallback.
If the gallery is slow, photo lookups are running for every row. Use initials in galleries and photos only on the detail screen.
If Coalesce still shows blank, the DisplayName is an empty string. Test the Email instead.
If the unassigned filter shows a delegation warning, add a text column that holds the owner's email and filter on that.

use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.shortDescription: Detect that someone else changed a record while the user had it open, and let them choose what to do.
use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.fullDescription: SharePoint rejects a Patch when the record has changed since it was loaded. This pattern checks the Modified time before saving, shows who changed the item and when, and offers reload or overwrite instead of a cryptic error.
use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.problemStatement: Two people edit the same item, and the second either overwrites the first without knowing or gets an error about a server conflict and loses their input.
whenToUse: Records edited by several people
Screens that stay open for a long time
Custom forms using Patch
whenNotToUse: Records only one person ever edits
Fields where the last write should always win
stepByStepInstructions: Store the record's Modified time when it is opened.
Before saving, read the item again and compare its Modified time.
If it is newer, show a dialog saying who changed it and when.
Offer reload, overwrite, or saving only the fields the user changed.
Update the stored time after every successful save.
commonMistakes: Patching the stale record from a variable, which triggers the conflict error.
Overwriting silently by always patching a fresh LookUp without comparing.
Showing the raw conflict error with no way forward.
troubleshooting: If every save reports a conflict, a flow updates the item right after each save. Refresh the stored Modified time after saving, or have the flow avoid touching the item.
If the conflict is never detected, the comparison uses a time captured after a refresh. Capture it only when the record is opened.
If the Editor name is blank, read it from the fresh LookUp rather than the gallery.
If the error text mentions an ETag mismatch, that is the same conflict reported by SharePoint. Use the fresh record as the Patch base.

use-a-reusable-validation-summary.shortDescription: Show every validation problem in one summary box at the top of the form, with a tap to jump to each field.
use-a-reusable-validation-summary.fullDescription: A validation summary tells users everything that needs fixing at once. This pattern defines the rules as a table, collects failures on save, lists them in a box and moves focus to the field when a message is tapped.
use-a-reusable-validation-summary.problemStatement: Users fix one error, press Save, and get the next one, several times in a row.
whenToUse: Forms with many fields or several sections
Accessibility requirements for clear error reporting
Custom forms and tabbed layouts
whenNotToUse: Two or three field forms, where inline messages are enough
Standard forms where the built-in card errors meet the need
stepByStepInstructions: Write every rule as a row with a key, a failing condition and a message.
On save, collect the failing rows.
Show them in a summary box above the form.
Move focus to the field when its message is tapped, switching tab if needed.
Drive inline borders and messages from the same collection.
commonMistakes: Showing errors before the user has tried to save.
Separate rule sets for the summary and the inline messages.
Messages that say a field is invalid without saying how to fix it.
troubleshooting: If SetFocus does nothing, the control is hidden or in a different container that is not visible. Switch tab first, as shown.
If the summary lingers after fixes, re-run validation on change.
If a date rule fires when the end date is empty, add a blank check to the condition.
If screen readers do not announce the summary, set the label's Live property.

use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.shortDescription: Define which status changes are allowed, and by whom, in one table that drives the buttons and the save check.
use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.fullDescription: A transition matrix lists each allowed move from one status to another with the role that may make it. The app reads it to offer only valid next steps and to validate before saving, so workflow rules live in one place.
use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.problemStatement: Items jump from Draft to Closed, or move backwards, because any status can be picked from a dropdown.
whenToUse: Workflows with more than three statuses
Rules about who can move an item
Rules that change over time
whenNotToUse: Two-state items such as open and closed
Workflows enforced entirely in a flow or in Dataverse business process flows
stepByStepInstructions: List every allowed move with its starting status, target status and role.
Work out which roles the user holds for the open record.
Show a button for each transition that matches the current status and the user's roles.
On click, check the status has not changed, then Patch the new status with who and when.
Keep the matrix in a list if the business needs to change rules without a new app version.
commonMistakes: A free status dropdown alongside the matrix, which bypasses it.
Rules coded separately on each button.
Not checking the current status again at the moment of saving.
troubleshooting: If no buttons appear, the item's status text does not match any From value. Check spelling and spaces.
If a user sees too many actions, their roles are calculated too broadly.
If the status is changed in the list directly, the matrix is not enforced there. Restrict list editing or add a flow that reverts invalid moves.
If the gallery of actions flickers, calculate roles once per record instead of inside the gallery.

use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.shortDescription: Show users a read-only summary of what they entered and ask them to confirm before the record is submitted.
use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.fullDescription: A review step catches mistakes before they reach approvers. The same screen switches into review mode: inputs become read-only text, a summary highlights key values, and the user confirms or goes back to edit.
use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.problemStatement: Requests are submitted with wrong amounts or dates, and correcting them after submission means a rejection and a resubmit.
whenToUse: Submissions that are hard to change afterwards
Forms with amounts, dates or declarations
Multi-step forms, as the final step
whenNotToUse: Quick forms where an edit after saving is easy
Forms that already save drafts and let users edit freely
stepByStepInstructions: Add a mode variable with Edit and Review values.
Validate when the user continues, then switch to review.
Show the entered values as read-only text, with consequences such as who will approve.
Require a confirmation tick before enabling Submit.
Let the user return to editing with their values intact, and save only on Submit.
commonMistakes: Saving the record before the review step, so cancelling leaves a submitted item.
A review screen that repeats the form without highlighting what matters.
Clearing the inputs when the user goes back to edit.
troubleshooting: If view-mode inputs are hard to read, use the separate summary container instead.
If values are lost on returning to edit, the review step is a different screen with its own controls. Keep both modes on one screen.
If Submit stays disabled, the confirmation checkbox was reset. Check its Reset is only called when going back.
If formatted values look wrong, such as dates in another language, pass a language tag to Text.
